Our proposed approach, Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), offers a novel way to
represent objects using 3D point clouds, independently of the orientation.
NDF generates a function that provides a pose-invariant descriptor for any
object point cloud, enabling comparison and classification. By training a 3D
neural network on a cloud representing an object in any orientation, NDF
achieves this invariance. Our method ensures the network's symmetry can be
maintained, using a SE(3)-equivariant neural network, thus ensuring the
generated descriptor is independent of the object's orientation. Experiments
demonstrate NDF's effectiveness on object classification and few-shot object
segmentation tasks, outperforming current methods while using significantly
fewer parameters. NDF also excels in handling real-world noise and diverse
poses, achieving near-human performance on the former and exceeding it on the
latter. By maintaining object orientation independence, NDF delivers
ground-breaking results in few-shot object segmentation. Code and models are
available at https://github.com/google-focalloss/Neural-Descriptor-Fields. 
We introduce the Few-Shot 3D Object Segmentation Benchmark, a first of its
kind, and present results for NDF on the ModelNet40 dataset. NDF's key
advantages over other methods include using the few-shot approach to extend
object classes, training on only 25 samples per class, and employing a
simple foreground-background segmentation method. This is particularly
accomplished on the VGG-SHAPES dataset, achieving high accuracy in 3D
classification and segmentation. NDF's unique features make it an innovative
solution for 3D object recognition and segmentation while providing a
flexible framework for learning about other types of shapes. This research
is an early exploration of Neural Descriptor Fields with numerous potential
extensions, including combining 2D and 3D data, using NDF for object
manipulation, and developing a 3D action recognition system. This paper is
being presented at the 2020 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern
Recognition (CVPR). NDF's papers can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.06618.

Recently, pose estimation has gained significant interest due to its practical applications, especially with the rise of artificial reality technologies. Establishing accurate correspondences between a 3D model and 2D image projections is a crucial challenge in estimating a model's degrees of freedom. Certain deep learning-based methods have demonstrated the ability to establish correspondences and estimate poses in a single step, yet they often struggle with increasing model complexity and varying poses. In contrast, traditional methods first project the 3D model onto the image and then cluster projections before determining the pose. Inspired by the strengths of both approaches, we present a novel two-stage pose estimation framework called DeepHMap++. The first stage utilizes a projection clustering network to establish a correspondence map by identifying clustered projections and determining the pose. The second stage, a correspondence learning module, leverages the correspondence map to establish additional correspondences and estimate the pose in an end-to-end manner. The proposed framework achieves superior performance on the CMU Pascal SIFT and ANTS datasets compared to existing deep learning-based methods. Furthermore, DeepHMap++ exhibits robust performance in estimating the full degrees of freedom for varying poses and complex models. The code for DeepHMap++ has been made publicly available on GitHub. In particular, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods like Cross-Modal Correspondence Network (CMCN) and Multi-task Graph Convolutional Network (MT-GCN) by a significant margin on the ANTS dataset, particularly when estimating poses for complex models. On the CMU Pascal SIFT dataset, DeepHMap++ delivers the best performance by a relatively smaller margin. Overall, our research demonstrates the efficacy of combining projection clustering and correspondence learning for pose estimation. In effect, DeepHMap++ sets a new high bar for the performance of deep learning-based pose estimation methods, especially when estimating the full degrees of freedom for complex models and varied poses. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address various Graphical Lasso issues, including estimating sparse inverse covariance matrices, sparsely structured precision matrices, and multiple sparsely connected matrices. GGLasso supports conventional Graphical Lasso with an L1 penalty and alternative generalizations such as Graphical Lasso with a nonconvex penalty, weighted Lasso, and log-determinant concave reformulation, among others. The software utilizes Cython and C++ interfaces to AMD's BLAS and LAPACK for efficient core computations, ensuring fast and stable performance. Additionally, GGLasso includes an intuitive and adaptable Python interface, leveraging existing Python statistics modules while providing a range of tools for visualization, preprocessing, and post-processing results. The library's flexibility allows for customization of solver parameters, structure imposition, and preprocessing, making it suitable for a broad range of Graphical Lasso applications. The source code of GGLasso is openly available on GitHub, alongside examples and a comprehensive user guide that can be found at https://gglasso.github.io/.

We tackle the issue of raw image noise and blurring caused by the readout process, shot noise, and photon shot noise, developing a novel demosaicking method that also handles deblurring and denoising of raw images. To facilitate better learning, we introduce a raw image deblurring demosaicking network (RIDDNet) that jointly learns demosaicking, deblurring, and denoising tasks. To provide realistic training data, we generate raw images based on clear images, considering the effects of the camera system, blurring, and noise. Evaluating our method against state-of-the-art raw image demosaicking approaches, we found it yields significantly better PSNR performance. Moreover, when applied to real-world raw images, our method outperforms existing raw demosaicking techniques in PSNR terms and produces visually more appealing results. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/zhengyangwang/RIDDNet. Furthermore, this work has been recognized with the Best Student Paper Award at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2020. When applying our method to real-world raw images, we observed significant time consumption, which we addressed by implementing several optimizations, resulting in a substantial reduction in training time without compromising performance. In this updated research, we introduce an alternative raw demosaicking approach that learns from simulated images, which facilitates easier model training. Compared to raw data-based methods, this approach offers the advantage of flexible system simulation, which we leveraged to explore novel demosaicking techniques. For instance, we explored demosaicking schemes with different filter patterns, such as ring and grid patterns, and found that our model can effectively generalize across various filter configurations. Moreover, we discovered that our model can seamlessly adapt to different noise levels, blurring extents, and camera system parameters, which significantly simplifies model selection. However, when hardware components are physically separated from other system parts, our research reveals that this setup frequently results in over-securing, as it often relies on outdated security standards. To address this issue, we developed a innovative method to quantify the level of trust required for hardware components that are isolated from the physical environment. This technique allows us to pinpoint the sources of unnecessary over-security and reduce them accordingly. In addition, we analyzed multiple hardware components and gathered insights into their respective trust requirements, along with proposing several efficient yet secure methods to revive outdated hardware. Our approach and resulting findings can serve as a foundation for reevaluating and refining the security policies governing computer systems. Furthermore, we incorporated our trust quantification framework into a system framework, which successfully demonstrated an average performance boost of 17% in user interactions and a maximum energy reduction of 11% for hardware components. Collective, our work highlights the importance of striking a balance between hardware security and over-security in computer systems. Additionally, it paves the way for a more nuanced exploration of the complex interplay between hardware security, energy consumption, and system performance. In the concluding section, we outline potential research extensions, along with a summary of our major contributions. Lastly, we introduced the concept of trust-aware hardware revitalization, which involves restoring outdated hardware to a more secure state while minimizing the level of trust required for its operation. Furthermore, we explored the possibility of applying our research to the revitalization of hardware in edge and cloud computing environments. Although these domains hold promise, our work is primarily tailored towards the revitalization of hardware within desktop and laptop computers. Therefore, we primarily utilized the hardware components and their respective trust requirements that are commonly found in these systems. Nevertheless, the idea of combining hardware revitalization with trust requirements could yield substantial benefits in securely meeting the ever-expanding processing demands of these computing environments. We investigate the challenge of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence extends across multiple episodes, as is the case in real-world situations, where it targets the policy gradient method by masking the underlying MDP. Notably, previous studies assumed that the attacker's goals are achieved by relatively small-scale corruptions, but in many actual scenarios, the rewards and transition probabilities can be greatly altered. Our research tackles this issue head-on by assuming the attacker's influence can result in substantial data corruption, potentially leading to a fully opposing MDP, yet only within individual episodes. Although the attacker's actions result in significant, episode-to-episode variations in rewards and transition probabilities, they remain bounded when averaged across episodes. Our primary contribution is a robust reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages the constraints of its target MDP to minimize the impact of corruption on the policy gradient estimate. This is possible because the algorithm bounds the norm of the corrupted transition probabilities' average, while also bounding the norm of the reward vector. As a result, we derive a robust policy gradient estimate that is independent of the number of episodes and has a bound that is linear in the episode length. This estimate is utilized within a robust optimization framework that involves a minimax optimization problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of our robust policy gradient algorithm, initially in a basic model and then in a more complex scenario, by comparing it to non-robust baseline approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/author-name/robust-pg. Notably, achieving strong data corruption presents significant challenges for simple methods like value-based reinforcement learning, prompting us to introduce a new challenge, robust reinforcement learning with transition reward corruptions, that offers a more manageable level of corruption, with resulting algorithms also worthy of publication. Finally, we investigate direct reinforcement learning approaches that learn robust value functions by implementing robust temporal difference learning, resulting in which the attacker's influence is mitigated through the use of robust TD learning that learns robust value functions by implementing the Kullback-Leibler divergence, with resulting algorithms also worthy of publication. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research to couple light with vibrational modes in crystals using excitons as a bridge.  While significant advances have been made, very few studies exist on excitons coupled to phonons, particularly those within self-assembled quantum dots, primarily due to difficulties in achieving the necessary conditions.  Recent breakthroughs in growing wurtzite nanowires have made it possible to site-control exciton-phonon couplings and implement all-optical manipulations.  Our experiments involve exciting quantum dots within nanowires at low temperatures using near-infrared pulses, allowing us to observe the interaction between a single photon and a mode in the nanowire.  Although expected to result in a steady state where the photon and mode are locked in a specific ratio, our measurements instead show vast variations in this ratio, often changing by tenfold within a millisecond, and exhibiting distinct patterns that shift every few nanoseconds.  Our findings indicate that these variations are caused by the large fluctuations in energy separation between the photon and mode, and can be controlled by adjusting the shape of the quantum dot to either increase or decrease these fluctuations by as much as five times, with the largest effect observed in a dark exciton state.  This level of control over coupled systems could potentially allow for the development of sensitive devices that detect even the smallest changes in a system, such as a crystal, and could have implications for the study of biological systems that rely on multi-phonon interactions.  This work is also relevant to the broader field of quantum physics, particularly the study of quantum systems that involve the interaction of light with matter. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies treat this task as a flat label sequence classification problem, despite the inherent hierarchical structure of entities. This approach overlooks the comprehensive structure of entities and fails to leverage their distinguishing features, such as positional information and types. To address this limitation, we propose a novel nested NER model that integrates the structural characteristics of entities, incorporating their inner structure, start and end positions, and types to aid in classification. Furthermore, we introduce the RENET dataset, a comprehensive and publicly available nested entity dataset, to facilitate evaluation and comparison of different nested NER approaches. Our proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on the RENET dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of a comprehensive structure parsing approach for nested NER. Moreover, we examine the role of structural features in NER and provide insights to guide the construction of high-quality nested entity datasets. Our research indicates that a comprehensive structure parsing model yields superior performance over baseline models, underscoring the significance of feature engineering in NER. According to our experiments, a well-crafted dataset with diverse structures is crucial for the robust evaluation of nested NER models. This is the first study to delve into the structural aspects of nested NER and provide a comprehensive structure parsing model for this task. This model serves as a foundation for subsequent research on nested relational named entity recognition. Furthermore, we explore the scope of our proposed model by examining its applicability to cross-entitiy recognition and pose this problem as a new research direction within the field of natural language processing. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the development of conversational systems and address issues they pose, our research focuses on automated testing. We leverage next-action models, incorporating contextual decisions, to design a suite of advanced testing tools. These tools facilitate systematic exploration, pinpointing of errors, and optimized interaction paths. Furthermore, they can conduct multiple conversations in parallel, making them exceptionally efficient. We showcase the effectiveness of these tools on two notable platforms and the results of our efforts are made available open-source for the community to utilize. This paper proposes a new framework for few-shot learning that views prototypes as representative class centroids and aims to minimize the average distance between data points and prototypes. In order to reduce the number of parameters, we apply prototype reduction through clustering, employing a mixture model consisting of multiple prototypes. As a result, our framework achieves compact and distinct prototypes by solving a mixture model under the K-means++ initialization. Before participating in classification tasks, our algorithm refines the prototypes by solving a linear system derived from least squares. We evaluate our method against several baseline models, including clustering-based prototype reduction and soft prototypes, achieving comparable performance in most cases while using significantly fewer parameters. As an added benefit, our method ensures that prototypes adhere to the original class labels. Our code is available for public review at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/clsfs.git. As for evaluation metrics, we employ standard few-shot learning metrics, including accuracy and Inception Score. Our experiments cover multiple scenarios, including 1-shot and 5-shot learning, as well as both single-shot and multi-shot learning. Our prototype learning approach demonstrates particular effectiveness in learning letters and symbols from the miniImageNet and 5-shot datasets. Moreover, our method successfully applies to self-supervised few-shot learning by leveraging data augmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the miniImageNet dataset. Our findings suggest that our method not only minimizes the average distance between data points and prototypes but also yields better performance than other few-shot learning methods. Our research also reveals that the number of prototypes learned has a direct impact on performance, with over-compact prototypes leading to suboptimal performance. As for potential drawbacks, our method may struggle with with large classes and low-resolution images. Our approach takes advantage of the fact that few-shot learning typically involves learning from small classes. Our work may also be susceptible to outliers, as it uses the mean square error as the loss function. As for the cluster number, we empirically determined an optimal range for our dataset, but this value may vary depending on specific datasets. These functions can be seen as a bridge between the user's problem formulation and the underlying optimization framework. We showcase our approach with examples of various conic types, including those arising from polynomial equations with a non-negative domain. Furthermore, we highlight that our method supports user-defined functions through either the Zygote or the Flux interface, making it suitable for differentiating his conic objects. Finally, we emphasize that our solution caters for a wide range of possible dimensions in both variables and parameters. The escalating demand for using MRI in clinical trials and research necessitates an efficient and reliable quality assurance process to ensure data uniformity and top-notch image standard. Human evaluators are currently responsible for assessing MRI quality but have inherent limitations, including subjectivity and exceptional costs. This study aims to introduce an automated quality assessment system to streamline and standardize the evaluation process. We leveraged a substantial and diverse dataset comprising over 110,000 MRI scans from various centers to develop and test our model. Our results demonstrate that a relatively small training dataset can enable the automated detection of poor-quality MRI scans with an AUC of 0.995, even when generalizing to unseen centers and patient populations. This achievement underscores the exceptional stability of MRI physics and the expertise of healthcare professionals responsible for operating and maintaining MRI systems. Our research provides a foundation for creating a versatile and adaptable automated quality assessment system that can efficiently ensure high-quality MRI data across multiple centers and sites. This innovative approach can also serve as a precursor to sophisticated learning tasks, such as predicting MRI contrast and segmentation mask quality. Furthermore, we explore the concept of multi-factorial generalization in the context of medical image analysis and introduce an automated quality assessment application that exemplifies this complex idea. This study showcases the value of robust, diverse datasets in conjunction with rigorous methodological strategies to ensure successful medical machine learning applications. Additionally, we explore the integration of our model into an existing MRI data management system and highlight the benefits of incorporating automated quality assessment into the imaging process. This research also emphasizes the importance of transparent reporting guidelines in medical machine learning, emphasizing the need for explicit discussion of data diversity, labeling methods, and quality assurance processes. This is particularly crucial for MRI data, which often involve intricate physical processes and sophisticated reconstruction techniques that necessitate a comprehensive understanding of MRI technology, hardware, and clinical procedures. This awareness is vital for fostering collaboration and knowledge sharing among cross-disciplinary teams working on medical imaging projects. These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The aim of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth exploration of the fundamental concepts and techniques in SPDEs. 

The chosen PDE model, the stochastic wave equation with additive white noise, serves as the primary example for demonstrating the applications of variational methods and the derivation of moment bounds, including the establishment of existence and uniqueness results for mild solutions and the determination of their long-term behavior. 

The lecture notes cover the basic theory of stochastic analysis, including the construction of the Wiener measure, the definition of Ito integrals, and the properties of Malliavin derivatives. 

The second chapter of the lecture notes delves into the derivation of weak solutions and the establishment of bounded moment norms for the wave equation. 

The final chapter of the lecture notes investigates the pathwise uniqueness of mild solutions and the application of the Basser-Kunita-Engelbert decomposition in determining existence and uniqueness. 

The lecture notes conclude with an exploration of the fractional Kirchhoff equation and its reformulation as a stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation. 

The appendix of the lecture notes provides supplementary material, including the derivation of the stochastic Harnack inequality, the proof of the Basser-Kunita-Engelbert decomposition, and the establishment of the fractional Kirchhoff equation's uniqueness. 

The lecture notes are intended for graduate students and early career researchers in the field of stochastic analysis and partial differential equations. 

The companion lecture notes for the second mini-course on stochastic PDEs can be found at the link provided.

This study explores the double longitudinal spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cos$\phi$ dependence of the asymmetry for the same-hadron and opposite-hadron cases when the jet and hadron are both mesons or both baryons. Using the color-glass condensate model, we calculate the interference function and the cos$\phi$ asymmetry for the two scenarios. When applying to heavy quark cases within the heavy quark effective theory, we derive the interference function's $\cos\phi$ dependence through an operator product expansion. This research is also extended to consider charm semi-inclusive deep dissociation. As a result, we can extract the wavelength-like dipole density of the $x$-density quark gluon plasma in semi-inclusive hadron production. Moreover, we demonstrate that the double longitudinal spin asymmetry in hadron pair production is driven by the interference between the quark and gluon twist-4 charm correlation functions. This understanding is then utilized to investigate the cos$\phi$ asymmetry when hadron pairs' transverse momentum is considered, and a corresponding expression is derived. Ultimately, with the development of experimental facilities such as the 12 GeV Jefferson Lab and the future construction of the Electron-Ion Collider, these theoretical predictions for the cos$\phi$ asymmetry in hadron pair production will be experimentally verified. Furthermore, with the ability to distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to heavy quark systems, these experiments will also shed light on the nature of the quark gluon plasma's influence on heavy quark phenomena. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation model that focuses on suggesting well-known historical figures for a given user query.
It leverages a layered Wikipedia knowledge base, utilizing the site's category hierarchy to enhance search results by integrating both lexical and taxonomic information.
To optimize performance, a novel approach combines a weakly-supervised approach with a diverse sampling method to effectively select and recommend entities from the Wikipedia database. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms existing Wikipedia entity recommendation techniques. Furthermore, we examine the effectiveness of our approach when applying the model to the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. As a result, this method has particular utility for modeling multiphase materials with complex geometries and boundary conditions. To validate this method, simulations of melting and solidification are provided, including cases involving discrete solid particles and irregular boundary geometry. Additionally, this method has been applied to model the casting solidification process of a titanium alloy, incorporating nucleation site selection algorithms to simulate grain growth. By leveraging this approach, complex grain structures similar to those observed in actual castings have been generated. This method has been implemented using the finite volume method and level-set equations, and with an example application, the method's performance has been evaluated in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. To accelerate policy optimization in batch reinforcement learning settings, experience replay has been effectively utilized by reusing a batch of random historical transitions to train a single policy. Nonetheless, the diversity of the used transitions significantly impacts the efficiency of optimization. In this study, we introduce a variance-reducing approach to enhance the diversity of experienced rewards for optimization. By leveraging the gradient variations, we propose two methods to select historical transitions that minimize the variance of value estimates, thereby improving the efficiency of optimization. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the standard experience replay method in various challenging reinforcement learning scenarios. Moreover, our approach achieves comparable performance to multiple sample-based methods while utilizing only a fraction of historical transitions, indicating a substantial reduction in required training data. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ghr35/VDRER.

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field reveal that the recovery of the NMR signal deviates from a single-exponential curve, indicating the presence of two distinct relaxation components with different temperature dependences. to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, we present a challenge for 
machine learning models to engage in complex conversations, maintaining high 
branching factors and coherent turn structures. Our best-performing model, 
achieved through sequential multi-round training, produces more diverse and 
coherent continuation branches than existing methods. Its strong performance is 
reflected in lower diversity scores when evaluated against the MultiTalk Dataset. 
Our study of conversational dialogue also highlights the challenge of high 
branching factors, implying that future research should prioritize diversity 
maintainence in smaller subsets of text. Our research and dataset are 
accompanied by readily usable code for further development of models in this 
domain. Additionally, we introduce DiversityAwareDecoding, an easy-to-implement 
trick for enhancing diversity in regular text generation tasks. This technique 
involved fluidly integrating various decoding strategies, ultimately yielding a 
strong baseline for our benchmark tasks. Nonetheless, our research shows 
that DiversityAwareDecoding under optimal decoding parameters still lags behind 
our primary model, MultiTalk, in terms of diversity and overall performance. 
Therefore, our study remains relevant even with the integration of this simple 
diversity decoding approach. Furthermore, we explore the scope of our study 
by expanding on previous research related to conversational dialogue, heavy 
branching, diversity, and the challenges faced by machine learning models in 
these domains. Our research is complemented by the inclusion of both 
qualitative and quantitative evaluation metrics for our dataset and models.

Our research is centered on enhancing the throughput of wireless communication networks by utilizing passive surfaces that change the propagation of radio signals. To provide accurate calculations, we take into consideration the effects of correlated signal strengths and irregular phase shifts. Utilizing this more precise approach, we perform statistical analyses and establish formulas to predict average network performance across various scenarios. In particular, we create mathematical models to calculate the probability of achieving optimal network speeds and formulate the average optimal speed as a function of key network characteristics. Through numerical simulations, we compare the performance of networks with passive surfaces to those that do not have them and find out how the shape and position of the surfaces affect them. Finally, we apply our models to analyze how passive surfaces can improve the performance of networks in real-world scenarios. To that end, we obtain general insights on how to design passive surfaces to maximize the optimal speed of a network. Furthermore, our models can be used to determine the optimal surface characteristics for a given network in practice. In contrast to existing research, our approach allows for the optimization of multiple surface characteristics, and we demonstrate this by finding the best settings for a a network with correlated signal strengths and irregular phase shifts. The models also enable us to explore different strategies for predicting average network performance and comparing the performance of different networks. Lastly, we discuss potential directions for further research on the optimization of wireless communication networks with passive surfaces. Through our research, we establish and analyze a mathematical model for predicting the optimal speed of a network, and we investigate how passive surfaces can improve the performance of a class of wireless communication networks. The model involves multiple surface characteristics and incorporates their effects on signal strengths, and we explore different strategies for predicting average network performance and comparing the performance of different networks. The models are applicable to a broad range of wireless communication networks with passive surfaces and provide a general framework for optimizing network performance. The model is relevant to a wide range of wireless communication networks, including those with correlated signal strengths, irregular phase shifts, and large arrays. The models can be used to determine the optimal surface characteristics for a given network and obtain general insights on how to design passive surfaces to maximize the optimal speed of a network. It is shown that for any given integer $k$ greater than or equal to one, $k$ independent stochastic evolution processes can be independently generated within the domain. Additionally, under certain conditions, a field defined by a conformal field theory can be shown to be equal to a specific multiple of a Gaussian free field. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source project that offers a customized version of the wiki software for use in research collaborations. WorkingWiki extends the capabilities of standard MediaWiki by providing a robust online framework that enables teams to work together on research projects, manage information, and share findings through a website. With its derivation from the base MediaWiki code, WorkingWiki retains all the core features and functionalities of a traditional wiki while incorporating additional tools to streamline research operations. These additional features encompass a modular layout for organizing content, a customizable start page for tracking progress, a dedicated section for showcasing publications, as well as integrated tools for managing citations and references. Furthermore, WorkingWiki is built with security and flexibility in mind, allowing users to easily install third-party extensions that cater to specific research needs and maintain the overall stability of the platform. By providing a comprehensive set of features and a secure environment, WorkingWiki is an ideal solution for hosting research projects using MediaWiki and its derivatives, including BioWiki and WikiPathway. Additionally, the source code of WorkingWiki is freely available for download from GitHub under the permissive BSD 3-Clause License. To explore the capabilities of WorkingWiki first-hand, a public demonstration site has been set up at https://workingwiki.org. Users can refer to the project's user manual located at https://workingwiki.org/wiki/index.php/Help:Contents for a step-by-step guide to getting started with WorkingWiki. A corresponding paper detailing the development of WorkingWiki has been published in the F1000Research journal at https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.13901.2. WorkingWiki is currently being utilized by the Collaborative Research Group at https://crg.rockefeller.edu, and is also an official partner of the BioWiki initiative. Users can reach out to the development team at workingwiki@rockefeller.edu for any inquiries or to explore potential collaborations. A dedicated issue tracker for the project is also available at https://github.com/rockefellerun/WorkingWiki/issues. To contribute to the project, please adhere to the guidelines outlined at https://github.com/rockefellerun/WorkingWiki/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md. A key feature of WorkingWiki is its ability to serve as a platform for conducting open science, and as such, the project is committed to upholding the principles of transparency and openness. As such, the project is registered with the OpenWorm Foundation's Meta-Wiki at https://meta.openworm.org/wiki/WorkingWiki. Working

We present a novel, flexible, and effective method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior in networks of interconnected neurons, including traveling chimera states and synchronized clusters. Our approach involves a straightforward, yet robust solution to determine node connectivity within the network, thereby facilitating the location of clusters and chimera states. By examining local phase relationships among neurons, our method can efficiently identify traveling chimera states. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach is insensitive to diverse initial conditions and reveals previously unseen aspects of traveling chimera states. Furthermore, we observe that both inner and edge nodes contribute to the formation and maintenance of traveling chimera states. Our work also shows that traveling wave patterns can emerge even when there is significant variability in the firing of individual neurons. Moreover, we find that our method is particularly adept at identifying traveling wave states over other approaches, such as comparing intranode phase differences with those between nodes. Lastly, we explore the impact of different firing rates on traveling chimera states and find that our method is equally effective regardless of these factors. Overall, our research reveals that traveling chimera states can occur even in networks with firing patterns that are far from identical, and that our method is an invaluable tool for a comprehensive understanding of these complex phenomena. Furthermore, we believe that our method can be adapted for use with other types of networks that feature interconnected units, such as graphs composed of coupled oscillators. Additionally, we explore the idea that traveling wave patterns may provide insight into the inner workings of large networks by allowing us to break down such networks into more manageable components, such as synchronized clusters, and that our method may be a useful instrument for exploring these types of networks. Furthermore, we discuss the possibility that our method could be used in conjunction with other techniques to gain a more nuanced understanding of traveling wave states, as well as the possibility that our method may be a suitable replacement for other approaches, such as methods that rely on the comparison of intranode phase differences with those between nodes, such as the method described in reference [9]. Additionally, we explore the idea that our method may be a suitable tool for use in experimental settings, such as in experiments involving the measurement of phase relationships among neurons in a network, as well as in numerical simulations, such as in simulations involving the firing rates of individual neurons, such as the simulations described in reference [10]. The extensive observation of gamma-ray lines above 10 GeV, indicative of neutral particles interacting with solar magnetic fields, remains a complex phenomenon to model. To address this, a comprehensive statistical analysis of solar magnetic field strengths was conducted, drawing from global solar magnetic field observations, and a linear regression model was developed to describe the relationship between the flux of isotropic ultra-high energy photons and solar magnetic field strengths. The model's ability to predict photon fluxes was validated through an independent data set, and its relevance was confirmed through a statistical assessment of correlations. The study found that the observed photon flux exceeding 10 GeV when solar magnetic field strengths are below 1 G, and the model can accurately predict such photon fluxes when solar magnetic field strengths range from 0.2 G to 1.5 G. However, a significant deviation from the model's predictions was observed for solar magnetic field strengths exceeding 10 G. Additionally, the study determined that the ratio of photon fluxes at 10 GeV and 50 GeV displays a similar linear relationship with solar magnetic field strengths, albeit with a different slope. The study's findings contribute to a better understanding of the complex phenomenon of gamma-ray lines above 10 GeV and the role of solar magnetic fields in generating isotropic ultra-high energy photons. The study further reveals that only solar magnetic field strengths in the range of 0.2 G to 10 G significantly contribute to the production of such photons. The study's results also raise questions regarding the production mechanism of neutral particles interacting with solar magnetic fields, suggesting that Compton scattering off low-energy solar photons may not be the predominant process generating isotropic ultra-high energy photons. Instead, the study suggests that other production mechanisms, such as pair production followed by the decay of mesic particles or the emission of photons by mesic particles, may contribute significantly to the observed photon flux exceeding 10 GeV when solar magnetic field strengths are below 1 G. The study further implies that only solar magnetic field strengths in the range of 0.2 G to 10 G can generate mesic particles with sufficient energy to contribute to the observed photon flux exceeding 10 GeV, and that the probability of detecting such particles with Cherenkov telescopes like HESS is very low, explaining the rarity of such events. Nonlocal gravity theory is a broad framework that can be applied across various spacetime metrics. This concept was initially introduced by von Loehneysen in 2007 and is based on nonlocal constitutive relations, which can be understood as responses from fundamental degrees of freedom that make up gravity. The purpose of this work is to review nonlocal gravity theory in depth, focusing on the underlying principles that fundamental degrees of freedom follow and the resulting constitutive relations that emerge from nonlocal interactions. A constitutive relation is a mathematical expression that defines a physical quantity in terms of other related quantities. The constitutive relations in nonlocal gravity theory are of this nature, describing how nonlocal gravity affects spacetime. The fundamental degrees of freedom that give rise to nonlocal gravity can be represented by field operators that apply to fundamental particles such as spin networks or Causal Dynamical Triangulation tetradons. The properties of nonlocal gravity can also be explored through semi-classical approximations of nonlocal constitutive relations, leading to modified Poisson equations that describe how nonlocal gravity impacts spacetime curvature. The choice of a specific nonlocal gravity theory depends on the constitutive relations used, which can be investigated through experiments that distinguish between different gravitational fields and the gravitational effects on motion within those fields. The constitutive relations in nonlocal gravity theory also provide insight into the nature of gravity within dense objects, such as stars, where nonlocal gravity may affect the object's curvature and the motion of objects within that curvature. The ultimate goal of this work is to establish a comprehensive understanding of nonlocal gravity theory, along with its underlying principles and the experimental tests that this theory predicts will occur. The term "theory" in nonlocal gravity theory represents a comprehensive framework that explains how nonlocal gravity affects spacetime, along with the physical quantities that define this effect. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addresses this challenge, dubbed "last-writer-wins," but it can result in lost updates. We've identified a more versatile approach to manage replicated data, incorporating conflict resolution strategies across various access patterns. Our framework, named Remove-Win, allows designers to create conflict-free replicated data structures using a set of high-level specifications. We demonstrate the efficacy of this design framework by applying it to implement two use cases: a distributed counter system and an aggregation tree. Our analysis showcases the versatility of our framework in producing efficient, conflict-free data structures. Further details on the Remove-Win framework and its implementations are available in the appended design and protocolling guidelines. We believe that our work will contribute to the advancement of distributed systems research. Additionally, we've incorporated a design language into our code to facilitate the creation of Replicated Data Structures. This language, named RDSL, enables clear and concise design expressions, making it easier to design and analyze Replicated Data Structures. RDSL is an open-source language that is adaptable to various programming languages, as we've found with Remove-Win, our design framework built using C++ and Redis. We've also explored possible optimization techniques for our design framework. Although our research is primarily theoretical in nature, we've investigated the practical applications of our design framework with the help of industry experts. Our work has been acknowledged by the research community, as evident from the citations in the appended reference section. We've conducted a thorough review of existing conflict resolution techniques in Replicated Data Structures but have also explored potential extensions to our design framework in the appended discussion section. Our design framework has been successfully demonstrated through the execution of a Redis protocol, named Redi, and the development of a prototype Redis database using C++. We've explored the scope for further innovation in Replicated Data Structures with our design framework. Although our design framework is generally efficient, there are scenarios in which it may not match the optimal solution, as we've demonstrated through the analysis of two use cases, a distributed counter system and an aggregation tree. Our design framework has been designed to be flexible and adaptable to various programming languages, as we've shown with the implementation of two use cases, a distributed counter system and an aggregation tree, using C++ and Redis. With a comprehensive approach like this, we were able to explore various aspects of genome function and shed light on the intricate relationships between genomics and GWAS. Our study revealed that many of the traits that have been extensively studied have shown significant association with regions of the genome that are actively used by cells to regulate gene expression, such as regions of engagement with histone modification patterns, with an average of approximately 18% of these regions associated with each trait. Additionally, we found that proteins involved in cell processes like signal transduction, tissue differentiation, and metabolism are often associated with many of the traits, with an average of about 28% of these proteins connected to each trait. Furthermore, when examining each trait individually, we found that certain factors like cell process, signal transduction, and tissue differentiation are linked with at least 20 different human traits, highlighting their universal importance in maintaining cellular functions and overall health. Our study is unique in its comprehensive analysis of genome function across 18 human traits and provides valuable insights that can be used as a foundation for further research into the intricate relationships between genomics and GWAS. Observations of the Galactic Centre have revealed a significant population of quiescent X-ray binaries that likely contain neutron stars. In the past, these systems emitted bright X-ray bursts from neutron star binaries, indicating that they contain a neutron star. However, the reason these systems are no longer producing such bursts is not well understood. One possible explanation is that the underlying physics has changed, specifically the temperature difference between the accretion disk and the neutron star, which no longer exceeds the break value, making it impossible to detect bursts. Another explanation is that the systems have shifted from an 'ADC' (neutron star) to 'B' type, where the X-ray bursts are produced by the star itself during its spin-down, and these systems are then only observable when their X-ray emission is significantly enhanced, resulting in what are classified as transient X-ray bursts. This study examines the time intervals between these transient X-ray bursts for the known samples of neutron star and black X-ray binary transients, and discovers that the distributions for the two types are significantly different, with the neutron star variants displaying shorter average intervals, consistent with the 'B' type explanation. If these systems are indeed 'B' type, then their large masses and compact object radii imply a high likelihood of gravitational wave detection in the future, and a unique characteristic of such a detection would be an irregular signal modulation related to the time interval between the systems' transient X-ray bursts. This prediction provides a new test for the 'B' type explanation, and a new reason to closely monitor the time interval variants for these systems. Furthermore, if these systems are 'B' type, then their time interval distributions may hold valuable information regarding the total population of such binaries in the Milky Way, and a new method is developed to estimate this population based on this information, with a best estimate being around 45,000 to 85,000 such systems, or a fraction of 10 to 20 times the population of similar pulsar binaries, and a ratio of 'B' to 'ADC' type of around 3 to 6. This study also offers a theoretical explanation as to why the time interval distribution of these systems is skewed, based on the principles of Poisson statistics and the likelihood of detecting a transient X-ray burst, and explores the potential for a similar time interval distribution in the detection of gravitational waves. Finally, if these systems are 'B' type, then their time interval distribution provides a new example of how the same physical phenomenon can give rise to different observational outcomes

To assess how gravity behaves at distance scales far beyond those currently explored in laboratory settings, researchers turn to the "wide binary test of gravity." This test involves observing wide binaries, which are binary star systems that are separated by significant distances. The motion of these systems in three-dimensional space allows astronomers to determine if their existing understanding of gravity is sufficient or if an alternative theory is required. A study recently published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society utilizes data from the APASS and PTF catalogs to conduct the wide binary test. By comparing observations to simulations of conventional binary systems under the influence of the Newtonian gravitational force and the gravitational potential of the Milky Way, researchers identified the most relevant factors affecting the motion of wide binary systems. A series of statistical assessments were performed to evaluate potential flaws in their study, including analyzing wide binary systems that were recently formed, accounted for any errors in calculating their age, and factored in any disturbances their orbits may have undergone. The results showed that wide binary systems conform to the expectations of standard gravity models, specifically those described by General Relativity and the laws of stellar evolution. Furthermore, the research uncovered that systems with ages exceeding one billion years exhibited mass deficits, which could be an indication of operating or dormant compact objects within these binary systems. Additionally, the study revealed slight discrepancies in the positions of wide binary systems, which could be caused by subtle interactions with the Milky Way's dark matter field or other external gravitational influences. Ultimately, by refining existing models of conventional binary systems and incorporating their own observational data, researchers determined that wide binary systems, at an age of one billion years and beyond, do not provide sufficient grounds to reject standard gravity theories. A/ASPAF, a new application for identifying wide binaries, was introduced as a tool for furthering this research. This study is significant because it involves vast datasets from the APASS and PTF catalogs, and as such, its results are expected to influence future wide binary searches, particularly those conducted by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. A/ASPAF's effectiveness was demonstrated on these systems, and as a result, this study should also contribute to the discovery of rare and exotic wide binaries. For instance, systems consisting of an evolved white dwarf and a companion that is still on the main sequence are typically found through wide binary searches. We demonstrate the significance of accounting for momentum in describing electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, which are commonly assumed to be isotropic. Using first-principles calculations, we analyze phonon dispersion relations and electron-phonon and spin-phonon interaction matrices for various materials, revealing that they are actually anisotropic in nature. This anisotropy arises due to distinct atomic arrangements in crystals, thereby providing a crucial underlying mechanism that underlies the anisotropic behavior observed in materials' physical properties. We further show that neglecting this anisotropy might lead to inaccuracies in the calculation of phonon dispersion relations and the strength of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions. We suggest that our approach is pertinent for comprehending the anisotropic distribution of energy and the resulting anomalies in momentum, as seen in phenomena like phonon-assisted superconductivity, topological phase transitions, and spin photovoltaic effects. Furthermore, our work is relevant for enhancing the performance of solar cells and the detection of phonons, spin currents, and superconducting state using spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy and other methods. We have specifically examined the anisotropic interactions in metals (potassium and copper), topological insulators (bismuth telluride and antimonide), and superconductors (tin, niobium, and copper oxide), as well as in transition metal dichalcogenides (molybdenum disulfide and tungsten diselenide), with anisotropy patterns that are governed by the specific arrangements of atoms within these materials. We have also shown that the anisotropy of phonon dispersion relations and electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions can be altered by applying external pressure, resulting in the shifting of specific modes and their coupling with electrons and spins in an anisotropic manner. We have demonstrated that our approach is crucial for an accurate understanding of the anisotropic behavior of physical properties in materials and the anisotropic distribution of energy in phenomena like phonon-assisted superconductivity, topological phase transitions, and spin photovoltaic effects. Additionally, this introduction includes an exploration of $\tau$-tilting theory's connections to local algebras, cluster-tilting theory, and Calabi-Yau algebras. Furthermore, recent advancements in $\tau$-tilting theory, including those concerning $\tau$-tilting dimension and Bautista's conjecture, will also be examined. Finally, future research directions within the field of $\tau$-tilting theory are discussed. Additionally, the material on recent research advancements and future directions is intended to benefit established researchers in the field. To tackle this, we introduce two novel tasks to measure the semantic variety of text within dialogues and the ability of models to produce diverse semantic states. Our evaluation reveals that current state-of-the-art neural models fall short in accomplishing these tasks and incorporating elements of the NLI task enhances their performance. Furthermore, we observe that neural models can replicate some form of inference in conversations but struggle to capture complex semantic diversity. Our findings also indicate that the best approaches for these tasks rely on sophisticated neural architectures and incorporate elements of neutral semantics. Our data and code are available for public accessivity. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning.  To fully comprehend the effect of rotation in low-mass stars, a thorough exploration of rotating low-mass stars with varying initial rotation rates and masses is essential.  This study introduces a numerical solution that extends Leblond, Charlebas, and Haday's break-up rotation rate formula, allowing for rotation rates up to mass-shedding limits, in addition to developing new expressions for the equatorial surface acceleration, polar surface acceleration, and angular velocity in order to simulate low-mass stars efficiently.  Using these formulas, the behavior of low-mass stars with various initial rotation rates and masses can be simulated up to their mass-shedding limits, providing insights into the physical characteristics of rotating low-mass stars.  This simulation method can also be applied to rotating sub- stellar objects, such as brown dwarfs, by adjusting the simulation limits accordingly.  To verify the accuracy of the simulation method, a comparison with existing data on rotating low-mass stars is conducted, followed by an exploration of new scenarios for rotating low-mass stars, including scenarios involving high rotation rates and mass loss processes.  The developed simulation method can be employed to track the evolution of rotating low-mass stars in various environments, such as in globular clusters, by integrating the simulation results with the characteristics of these environments.  This research lays the groundwork for a comprehensive examination of the internal structure of rotating low-mass stars through numerical simulation, uncovering new features of rotating low-mass stars and demonstrating the effects of rotation on low-mass stars, a key area of study in the field of stellar astrophysics.  To facilitate the use of this simulation method, an executable code is made available for download, enabling users to simulate rotating low-mass stars through a user-friendly interface.  Future enhancements to this research will focus on enhancing the simulation method to account for the breakdown of hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars and developing a new simulation method for rotating low-mass stars that undergo mass loss processes.  In the meantime, this study provides a significant contribution to the field of stellar astrophysics by offering a simulation method that can accurately model the internal structure of rotating low-mass stars through numerical simulation, a crucial area of study in the field of stellar astrophysics. The continuous nature of real-world classification tasks necessitates the ability to continuously learn from streaming data.  Many algorithms have been developed to tackle the task of incremental learning, especially those that handle class incrementation.  However, a significant challenge arises when encountering imbalanced data, as the inherent disparity in class frequencies can hinder learning and accuracy.  Consequently, the development of calibrated algorithms to manage the shifting imbalance is crucial.  Our research extends beyond mere evaluation of the performance of iCIL algorithms, instead delving into a comparative analysis of various calibration methods that leverage min-clip calibration, virtual distribution matching, and maintaining a memory buffer to adapt to imbalanced data.  We introduce the concept of an imbalance pattern to describe the change in imbalance levels over time and assess the efficacy of different calibration methods under distinct patterns.  Through extensive experimentation on multiple scenarios representing different imbalance patterns, our research provides a comprehensive evaluation of the effectiveness of different calibration methods in the iCIL setting.  Our findings highlight the importance of selecting calibration methods that align with the underlying imbalance pattern, as this choice can either exacerbate or mitigate the performance gap by up to $21\%$ in our experiments.  Our research is relevant to categories such as action recognition, text classification, and medical diagnosis, where data is often imbalanced and learning is a continuous process.  We anticipate that our analysis will guide the development of more effective algorithms capable of learning from streaming data in the presence of varying imbalance levels.  We also introduce the first publicly available imbalanced incremental learning benchmark, consisting of six challenging scenarios that incorporate different imbalance patterns, along with evaluation protocols tailored to assess the performance of iCIL algorithms under controlled imbalance conditions.  This benchmark provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for the research community to address the challenging task of imbalanced class incrementation learning.  We validate the efficacy of our proposed approach through the development of an open-source code, featuring our first baseline algorithm that combines the capabilities of both expiring memory and recent data learning.  Our results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art iCIL algorithms by up to $12\%$ in our benchmark datasets.  Our research is an initial exploration into the comparative analysis of various calibration methods for managing data imbalance in the iCIL setting, and we anticipate that our findings will motivate further research into the development of more effective algorithms capable of learning from streaming data in the presence of varying imbalance levels. To do this, we consider a scenario where a Higgs-mediated diagram is significant, with an underlying theory that includes a Higgs field and incorporates a muon mass term via a dimension-five operator. Since this configuration violates lepton number, it likely requires a new physics scale to restore lepton number, which would typically imply that this contribution is unlikely to resolve the $\alpha_\mu$ anomaly. However, we show that if this new physics scale is related to the Higgs boson's mass scale ($\sim 1$ TeV) rather than the electroweak scale, the muon mass term's origin could plausibly be attributed to the Higgs field, thereby providing a coherent, multi-dimensional contribution to $\alpha_\mu$. Ultimately, we find that, although it requires a relatively heavy Higgs mass, a Higgs-driven solution to the $\alpha_\mu$ anomaly still remains feasible. Furthermore, this solution could be distinguished from other multi-loop, SM extensions by the Higgs characterization through Precision Global Anomaly Hunting, a proposed experiment that would offer a complementary approach to resolving this anomaly. Moreover, we find that this experiment's required muon flux is comparable to, yet still significantly lower than, the required flux for the proposed muon-electron collision facility. Lastly, we note that even if this Higgs-driven solution is not found, it would not rule out other multi-loop, SM-compliant solutions to the $\alpha_\mu$ anomaly. Ultimately, resolving this discrepancy will continue to provide rigorous, precision tests of the Standard Model. Furthermore, even if it takes an experimental resolution of approximately $10$ parts per billion ($10^{-10}$), it will remain one of the most scrutinized, precisely examined, and extensively theoretically interpreted anomalies in the history of particle physics. This study investigates the potential of transferring U-Net-based cardiac segmentation models, trained on images from healthy adults, to medical teams who require detailed segmentations for surgical planning involving rare congenital heart defects. Given that a significant portion of pediatric cardiac surgeries are performed on children with rare heart conditions, and the scarcity of pediatric cardiac MRI data, the proposed approach aims to facilitate access to accurate segmentations. Through the use of automated measurement tools and clinical expert assessments, the performance of transferred models was evaluated on a subset of 3D MRI data from 8 distinct congenital heart diseases, using both 2D and 3D U-Nets. The results showed that 3D U-Nets outperformed their 2D counterparts, yielding a mean surface distance of 4.07 mm, whereas 2D U-Nets achieved a mean distance of 5.05 mm. Furthermore, a 3D U-Net demonstrated comparable performance to a model trained on pediatric data, with a mean surface distance of 3.41 mm. This research provides initial evidence for the efficacy of transferring U-Net-based cardiac segmentation models to a broader range of rare congenital heart diseases. To build upon these findings, the paper outlines a pathway for further work, including the incorporation of multi-modal data and robustness testing against various external models. Moreover, the study highlights the value of collaborative efforts between medical professionals, researchers, and the broader deep learning community to accelerate advancements in this area. This research focuses on enhancing the reliability of numerical simulations for heterogeneous materials by addressing the inherent issues related to gradient-enhanced models. Heterogeneous materials exhibit characteristic size effects due to the distribution of inclusions, which influence their fracture and damage behavior. Existing models, such as power-law and exponential gradient models, have been developed to capture these size effects, but they often lack a clear connection to the characteristics of the material microstructure. As a result, these models can lead to unrealistic predictions and diminish the effectiveness of numerical simulations. In contrast, the proposed exponential and power-law gradient models utilize the material's characteristic length and R\" ucksack length to describe the transition between fracture and damage regions, thus providing a more nuanced understanding of damage evolution. Additionally, these models facilitate the use of higher-order numerical approximations without introducing artificial stiffness issues. Furthermore, the proposed models establish a clear link between the material's microstructure and the model's parameters, enabling their determination through inverse identification. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a more precise and reliable numerical framework for modeling the damage behavior of heterogeneous materials. As such, two-dimensional numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed models, and their results are compared to those obtained using traditional power-law and exponential gradient models. The research findings demonstrate that the proposed models yield more accurate results, particularly when using finer mesh sizes. As such, these models offer a more reliable and precise approach to modeling the damage behavior of heterogeneous materials. The research is further expanded to investigate the models' performance in capturing crack growth in three-dimensional simulations. The proposed models demonstrate a significant improvement in predicting crack paths when compared to their two-dimensional counterparts. By analyzing the underlying mathematics, a solution is found to yield a significant decrease in the required peak power, along with a balanced contribution of modes that reduces the required power by a factor of $\cal{N}$, where $\cal{N}$ represents the number of modes. A molecular ion, with certain vibrational modes connected by transition frequencies, is used as the test case, and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in maintaining frequency stability despite technical imperfections. The optimal gate duration is shown to be insensitive to minor frequency fluctuations and certain types of connection strengths between modes. The proposed balanced multi-mode approach addresses the issue of power-knot formation and provides a feasible path to implementing Molmer-Sorensen gates efficiently and accurately. The associated photon-spreading effects can be managed through partial application of mode transfer, leading to a significant improvement in gate duration. The new method holds promise for achieving Molmer-Sorensen gate fidelities greater than 99.9% for up to 128 modes within a 100-KHz frequency range, and with peak-power requirements that are only slightly above typical experimental values. The study of bimodal rates and proportions has long been a subject of interest in the statistics community, with numerous applications across fields like medicine, psychology, and social sciences. A valuable framework for inferences in this area has been developed using the delta method, yet its limited effectiveness for rate data has been a notable drawback. This article presents an alternative framework, based on asymptotic theory, to analyze bimodal rate and proportion data. This new approach addresses the challenges posed by traditional methods and provides a comprehensive framework for estimating and assessing bimodal distributions of proportions and rates through consistent parameters, empirical variance estimators, and quantile-based measures, ultimately facilitating hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction. This article also explores the performance of these methods via Monte Carlo simulations and a concrete example from the literature. Furthermore, a publicly accessible R package, bmstat, has been developed to execute the proposed methods and is available for download. This article provides a thorough review of the study of bimodal rates and proportions, along with a detailed examination of the theoretical framework and the results obtained from simulations and real-world data. In addition, potential future research directions on this topic are also discussed. In a quantum field theory context, the spectral shift anomaly in Sagnac interferometer geometry has been investigated. This analysis shows that the spectral shift anomaly displays frame dependence, exhibiting distinct behaviors under Galilean transformations. A comparative study is made with the anomaly's behavior in other geometric configurations, such as the Einstein-Rosen bridge and the Kerr black hole horizon, revealing that Sagnac interferometer unique properties arise from the specific anti-symmetric and closed nature of its cross-sectional surface. A deeper examination of this phenomenon is facilitated through a generalized analysis of spectral shift anomalies in curved spacetime settings. A key observation from this analysis is that the spectral shift anomaly's sign is defined by the scalar curvature of the surface in question, implying that all conformally equivalent geometries exhibit analogous spectral shift anomaly behavior. This framework is then applied to evaluate spectral shift anomalies in various settings, including both flat and curved spacetimes. A notable outcome from this investigation is the derivation of a spectral shift anomaly formula applicable to any closed and simply connected spacetime curve, providing a clear physical interpretation of the anomaly through a quantum interference resonance phenomenon. This analysis also reveals that the spectral shift anomaly is a resolvent expansion convergence rate determinant, with implications for Sagnac interferometer applications in both physics and engineering. This research also explores possible connections between spectral shift anomalies and both Hawking radiation and black hole entropy, presenting a new approach to these longstanding issues. A one-factorial spectral shift anomaly effect is predicted to occur in multicomponent systems, enabling the detection of extrinsic spectral shift anomalies, with potential applications in both physics and engineering. A review of the historical development of Sagnac interferometer physics highlights the pivotal role of spectral shift anomalies in understanding this phenomenon, concluding that the unique properties of Sagnac interferometer can be accounted for by the anomalous behavior of spectral shift operators. Finally, this study explores the implications of spectral shift anomalies for both general and special relativity, demonstrating that these theories can be modified to accommodate anomalies, with potential experimental verification awaited in the near future. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a challenging task due to variations in lighting and the need for comprehensive feature extraction. This difficulty is compounded by image quality issues, misaligned or occluded faces, and differences between male and female faces. Existing methods often employ multi-task learning and recurrent models but can be vulnerable to initial condition variations and broken feature extractions. This paper introduces a self-alignment dual face regression network that simultaneously processes pairs of male and female face images and uses a recurrent model for partial face reconstruction. This hybrid approach allows for independent feature extraction and promotes robust alignment and reconstruction across three dimensions. This technique is compact, efficient, and easy to train, yielding a 3D face reconstruction with 69 million parameters. This is significantly less than previous models, with a parameter count closer to that of two-dimensional face reconstruction models. This network achieves high accuracy on the WFU and FRGC datasets with mean distances of 2.12 and 2.55, respectively, outperforming previous methods by a margin of 0.12 on the WFU dataset. This approach also demonstrates robust performance in the presence of occlusions and misalignments. This method's efficiency and resilience make it an attractive solution for real-world face analysis applications. We investigate the consequences of symmetries being broken down from full de Sitter isometry $O(4, 2)$ to $O(3, 1)$ on the behavior of objects we call "fractons." These fractons have massless galvanic modes similar to those found in systems with full de Sitter symmetry but also exhibit additional low-energy properties. Our research shows that if translation symmetry is broken, the energy of a fracton can be reduced to that of a scalar field, but if other symmetries are broken, the energy remains that of a conformally coupled scalar field. Our work provides the bare parameters required to relate fracton behavior to that of a scalar field and demonstrates that the low-energy modes of fractons can be represented as a combination of a scalar field and a Goldstone boson. Furthermore, we derive the equation that describes the mode of a fracton in both its low-energy and high-energy forms. Our research also identifies two types of fracton systems: those with self-interacting fractons that can transition between low-energy and high-energy modes, and those with "locked" fracton monopoles that can only exist in their low-energy form. Our work provides the efficient field theory description for systems that feature fracton-like low-energy modes. It provides the Lagrangian approach to describe these systems in a more intuitive way and offers a bridge between the existing literature on systems with full de Sitter symmetry and those with broken symmetry. It also offers a preview of the broader class of systems that feature low-energy modes with constrained mobility. Our work offers a language that can be used to discuss these systems in an abstract way, focusing on their symmetries rather than their specific details. It allows us to identify a fundamental dichotomy in the behavior of these systems, and it offers a glimpse into what aspects of these systems could be experimentally probed. To tackle this, a novel, comprehensive deep learning architecture that incorporates a complete attention bidirectional sequence labeling framework is proposed in this paper. The proposed model builds upon previous bidirectional designs by leveraging a complete attention mechanism to process both input vector features and target label probabilities. We establish a new type of polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal link polynomial, specifically designed for links composed of n twisted toroidal components in a thickened torus. This novel polynomial construction is based on a specific combinatorial formula, analogous to the Jones polynomial's construction using the Kauffman bracket, but with an altered decknearization process. Furthermore, we prove that the volume hypothesis is applicable to the nth toroidal link polynomial, resulting in a unique, irreducible, and indecomposable invariant. This property enables the n toroidal link polynomial to distinguish between certain links that cannot be differentiated by the volume hypothesis in their classical form. Additionally, we explore connections between the n toroidal link polynomial and other established invariants, including the Jones polynomial and the Kauffman polynomial, revealing a relationship between them. This relationship is utilized to analyze the n toroidal link polynomial's properties, specifically its growth rate and combinatorial behavior. Moreover, we provide a preliminary evaluation of the n toroidal link polynomial's properties for specific links, including twisted toroidal versions of the trefoil, figure-eight, and Hopf links. This research provides a foundation for exploring potential connections between the n toroidal link polynomial and other invariants, such as the volume conjecture. This is especially evident in the case of the twisted toroidal trefoil, which demonstrates growth rate characteristics consistent with the volume conjecture's predicted behavior. This discovery, combined with the twisted toroidal link polynomial's volume hypothesis behavior, supports further investigation into this conjecture's validity. This is particularly relevant as the twisted toroidal version of the trefoil's volume hypothesis-inequivalent link can only be distinguished by this new polynomial.
