We present an open-source software suite, RCSED, for creating data visualizations of imaging and spectral observations. This development builds upon previous work by multiple authors, specifically leveraging the code contributed by J. G. Stangl (point source viewer), M. M. Perez (spectral dispersion diagram generator), and M. A. B. B. Santiago (2D imaging simulator viewer), with further enhancements incorporating Bootstrap and D3.js frameworks. Our updated version, RCSEDv2, incorporates additional features while maintaining cross-browser compatibility and ease of use. It comprises three primary tools: a point source viewer with customizable parameters and output options, a spectral simulator and analyzer for evaluating data fitting and residual fitting, and a 2D imaging simulator viewer for processing and visualizing data. Furthermore, RCSEDv2 includes a central repository that manages plugin libraries, enabling seamless integration of new features. The software is designed to be adaptable for various purposes, including educational initiatives and scientific project management. We invite the scientific community to contribute to and make use of this open-source platform. The Southern Atlantic rift system, extending from 3°N to 45°S latitude, developed as a divergent plate boundary where Africa and South America separated from Europe, North America, and Africa/South America, respectively, over a period of roughly 60 million years during the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. A kinematic analysis of this rift system has been conducted using a range of geological observations and data, with the goal of reconstructing its evolution. Initial rifting in the South Atlantic occurred at 132-129 million years ago in the South Atlantic, with associated extensional deformation observed in both Africa and South America. Estimates of pre-breakup relative motion between these two continents suggest 2-3 megameters of shortening and 1-2 megameters of crustal thinning. Prior to complete separation, these two continents moved apart at a slow rate of about 1 centimeter per year for about 40 million years, with associated deformation seen in both Africa and South America. Following this phase, South America continued to move northwestward towards its current position, with the two continents breaking apart at a faster rate of about 3 centimeters per year for about 20 million years. A growing concern in medical research is the limited availability of annotated images for training machine learning models, particularly in cases where labeling patient data is expensive, time-consuming, or impossible due to the high cost of obtaining accurate segmentations. One promising approach to overcome this limitation is to employ self-supervised learning, which enables machine learning models to be trained and fine-tuned on medical image segmentation tasks without annotated data. One self-supervised learning technique involves using latent space constraints to ensure that latent representations of input images and their masked counterparts are identical, thereby learning meaningful features that capture the underlying geometry of anatomical structures. However, this method has limitations because it relies solely on internal consistency within the latent space and ignores the boundary information that is critical to segmenting structures with distinct geometries. To address this, we propose a novel framework that incorporates boundary-sensitive information maximization to guide the learning of feature extractors. By leveraging both latent and boundary information, our framework achieves superior performance in medical image segmentation when compared to existing self-supervised learning methods, as evidenced by results from extensive experiments conducted across multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our approach facilitates efficient training by reducing the gap in segmentation accuracy between self-supervised and annotated models, thus demonstrating the effectiveness of boundary-sensitive information maximization in medical image segmentation. Additionally, we explore different hyperparameter settings and provide insights into the role of pre-training, while also applying our framework to real-world scenarios, including the semi-supervised setting, across various anatomical structures. Overall, our proposed framework outperforms competing self-supervised learning methods, achieving a significant boost in segmentation performance, and can be an invaluable tool for researchers and practitioners in medical image analysis. As such, we make our code and configuration publicly available to facilitate replication and advancement of this research. Through extensive experiments and qualitative analysis, we demonstrate the potential of our framework to adapt to different hyperparameter settings, generalization to diverse anatomical structures, and seamless integration with real-world scenarios, including the semi-supervised setting. Our proposed solution involves two primary components: a method for the Dungeon Master to understand player objectives and the game's theoretical framework, along with a neural language generation system that maintains a balance between creative, engaging storytelling and clear, concise exposition. The GNS construction forms a functor from the category of C*-algebras to the category of Hilbert spaces that represents the equivalence classes of C*-algebras under *-isomorphisms. This process involves three key components: a C*-algebra A, a unitary vector called the ground vector, and a map called the linearisation that establishes an isomorphism between A and the quotient of the space of linear operators by the ideal generated by the self-adjoint operators with zero kernel. The linearisation can be seen as a 2-dimensional vector consisting of the ground vector and the quotient map. It follows that the image of A under the GNS construction is determined by the ground vector and the linearisation, with the ground vector serving as the object component and the linearisation acting as both the 1-dimensional morphism component from A to the space of linear operators, as well as the 2-dimensional composition component from A to the quotient space. This relationship can be expressed through a natural transformation that relates the pre-Algebra functor to the quotient functor by the ideal of self-adjoint operators with zero kernel. It further follows that the equivalence classes of C*-algebras under *-isomorphisms can be represented by the quotient of the space of linear operators by the ideal of self-adjoint operators with zero kernel, with the ground vector providing a representation of the class. This representation of the class can be achieved through the application of the linearisation map, with the resulting 2-dimensional vector consisting of the ground vector and the quotient map. It is then possible to recover the original C*-algebra A by applying the inverse of the linearisation map to the 2-dimensional vector, with the ground vector serving as the object component and the quotient map acting as both the 1-dimensional morphism component from the space of linear operators, as well as the 2-dimensional composition component from the quotient space. Our findings show that the gamma-rays in these galaxies are correlated with their X-ray emission, which is likely generated by a restricted accretion disk surrounding a supermassive black hole. However, the relationship between gamma-rays and the emission of these galaxies in the ultraviolet, X-rays, and radio frequencies does not follow a simple linear pattern. Furthermore, we discover that the orientation of these galaxies does not significantly impact the observed correlation between gamma-rays and X-ray emission. This suggests that an orientation effect is not the primary factor in the observed correlation, and that other effects, such as electron acceleration in a restricted disk or in a potential jet, may be more influential in generating high-energy gamma-rays in these galaxies. Additionally, we find that the observed gamma-ray energy in these galaxies is relatively low, suggesting that a mechanism similar to that occurring in blazars, which have jets pointing directly at Earth, is not the dominant process at work. By integrating anchor points representing typical sample conditions into the training data, our approach enhances model performance on temporally restricted and high-dimensional sequences, significantly improving its ability to accurately model life science measurements for substances like RNA expression and pharmacokinetic curves. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek domain knowledge to inform their work, typically asking basic questions about existing research, future research directions, or new data analysis methods. Current technologies, such as search engines and expert discussions, can provide general overviews but often fail to address the nuances of these queries. In contrast, expert conversations often revolve around these same simple questions, suggesting that they have already been effectively answered through collaborative discussion. This paper proposes a novel idea: to anticipate future research conversations by first compiling a dataset of question-and-answer pairs that are derived from these discussions and rooted in underlying research papers. To validate this concept, we conducted an assessment involving both human evaluators and automated tools to ensure the quality of both our proposed model and the newly created dataset. Specifically, we utilized both explicit and implicit evaluation methods to test the practical applications of our proposed model, as well as its theoretical foundations. The model has shown promising performance in multiple metrics, such as overall accuracy, backward retrieval capability, and diversity in answer generation. In the process, we also identified several potential issues related to conversational dialogue, including problems with both initiation and progression. In the end, we observed that certain topics that are crucial to the field in question are surprisingly underrepresented in our proposed model. To facilitate further exploration and verification of our proposed concept, we have made both our model and the accompanying dataset freely available to the research community. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical modeling choices, including the SIR model and its derivatives. A unified framework incorporating critical epidemiological parameters, model specifications, and their implications on modeling the epidemic's peak and final epidemic outcome is established. Analyzing previously published models using this framework provides valuable insights for policymakers, highlighting the importance of transparent model disclosure to facilitate a deeper understanding and critique of modeling decisions in the context of evolving pandemic scenarios. Ultimately, this perspective emphasizes the value of collaborative dialogue between mathematicians and public health officials to develop practical solutions and predictive tools for addressing the complexities of infectious disease outbreaks. This review is an extension of a previous discussion presented at the 17th Conference on Mathematical Modeling of Biophysical Phenomena. Moreover, the epistemic and ontological underpinnings of modeling infectious disease dynamics are explored in an accompanying philosophical commentary. This study employs rapid magnetic resonance imaging to investigate temperature variations in a gas-solid fixed bed during an exothermic reaction.  We demonstrate that spatially resolved temperature maps can be obtained in mere seconds, enabling the capture of complex temperature patterns resulting from fluid flow and particle reactivity. By correlating temperature data with flow patterns, our research reveals intense thermal fluctuations develop near the bed's surface and at its center. These fluctuations are exacerbated under increased airflow conditions. A corresponding increase in surface reactivity with higher airflow also amplifies thermal fluctuations. Notably, a distinct temperature arrangement emerges in the upper bed region, exhibiting a molar reactivity order that contradicts the overall reactivity pattern. This disparity is attributed to varying residence times and reactant concentrations within the bed. This work showcases the versatility of rapid MRI in studying complex, dynamically shifting phenomena within confined environments. Additionally, it provides valuable temperature distribution insights in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially informing the optimization of industrial processes that utilize these beds. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential of MRI as an in situ monitoring tool, unintrusive and noninvasive, that can be employed to study reaction dynamics and flow patterns within these beds. This knowledge can also be applied to improve the design of fixed beds used in membrane reactors and catalytic converters. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A BDDC solver and an AMG solver were applied to determine the impact of different preconditioners on the convergence of a Newton-Krylov method. The study examined how initial conditions, muscle fiber orientation, and material properties affect solution times. Furthermore, both implicit and explicit cardiology applications were tested across a range of grid sizes and number of processor used. The research utilized a cardiac mechanics code with over 1 million degrees of freedom and was performed on up to 1024 processors on the Gordon supercomputer. The findings suggest that both scalable solvers can effectively solve large-scale cardiac mechanics problems, with slight variations in performance resulting from different finite element mesh configurations, muscle fiber orientation, and heart muscle material properties. The study demonstrates that both BDDC and AMG can be reliable and flexible tools for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on massive supercomputers. The research also highlights the need for further investigation into how heart muscle mechanics analysis can be efficiently implemented on exascale computers, especially in terms of future limitations and potential breakthroughs, as well as the value of using high-performance computing to better understand heart muscle dysfunction. The study was conducted using the NIH National Heart Biomechanics through Simulation (N2B2) grant and the computing resources were provided by the University of Minnesota Supercomputing Institute and the Texas Advanced Computing Center. The research was performed in accordance with the principles of the Fair Credit Reporting Act. The code used in the research is based on an unstructured tetrahedral finite element method developed in collaboration with researchers from the Mayo Clinic, the University of Minnesota, and the University of California, San Diego. The method was initially tested using a right ventricle mesh with approximately 160,000 nodes and 320,000 tetrahedral elements, as well as an left ventricle mesh with approximately 260,000 nodes and 540,000 tetrahedral elements, and was later scaled up to a total of over 1 million degrees of freedom. The study was performed on a Gordon supercomputer, a IBM NeXtScale and PowerIX-based cluster consisting of 2048 nodes, with each node featuring a 16-core Intel Xeon E5

The growing reliance on encryption technologies to ensure confidentiality of communication has sparked concern about the rising threat of side-channel information leakage. As a result, research has focused on quantifying the security risks associated with these side channels. This paper diverges from this approach by taking a measure-theoretic view of side-channel information, treating it as a form of noise that threatens encryption confidentiality. Building on this premise, we examine the impact of side-channel information on an attacker's probability of successful decryption, ultimately framing the associated security risk as a problem of information-theoretic security. Furthermore, we illustrate this concept through a specific example involving a false feeling of security in stream ciphers. The example is underpinned by a mathematical analysis and supported by empirical evidence from real-world implementations, namely the Rice Wheat stream cipher and the AES protocol, as well as their respective hardware implementations. The findings suggest that the risk of side-channel information leakage can exceed the risk of cryptanalytic attacks, highlighting the need for a more nuanced view of security that takes into account the interplay between side channels, cryptography, and performance. The paper concludes by exploring potential avenues for mitigating this risk, including the development of robust security metrics, the optimization of side-channel resistance in stream ciphers, and the exploration of false positive security as a new attack vector. Recent studies have identified a striking reversal in the star formation rate (SFR) sequence at the upper end of the main sequence. To shed light on the underlying causes of this phenomenon, we undertook a comprehensive analysis of the SFRs of massive galaxies using spatially resolved star formation rates from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ treasury survey. Our findings indicate that nuclear starbursts are prevalent in massive galaxies, with 80% of those above $M_{\rm bulge} \sim 10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$ displaying nuclear activity. Furthermore, we discovered a significant correlation between the mass of the nuclear starburst and the bulge mass, with nuclear starbursts exhibiting mass ranges of $10^7 M_{\odot}$ to $10^9 M_{\odot}$. Our study reveals that nuclear starbursts contribute substantially to the mass-to-starration ratio and account for the downturn of the sequence at high masses. Our analysis also delves into bulge formation through mergers, considering models of gas-rich mergers, with findings that such interactions can result in nuclear starbursts with mass-to-starration ratios similar to those observed. Ultimately, our study suggests that nuclear starbursts play a key role in determining mass-to-starration ratios in massive galaxies, with mergers potentially driving the observed sequence turn-over at high masses. Our research provides a deeper understanding of the interplay between star formation, mass accumulation, and nuclear activity in massive galaxies, with implications for the broader galaxy population. Furthermore, our study sheds light on the complex interplay between galaxy evolution, nuclear activity, and the observed sequence turn-over at high masses, with nuclear starbursts acting as a key bridge between these processes. Our analysis also explores the potential for quasar feedback in shutting down nuclear starbursts and star formation, with implications for the cooling and merging of gas. Our study paves the way for a more in-depth exploration of the interplay between galaxy evolution, nuclear activity, and the observed sequence turn-over at high masses, with a better understanding of the role of mergers in driving nuclear starbursts and the mass-to-starration ratio sequence turn-over. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of considering nuclear starbursts when investigating the sequence turn-over at high masses, with implications for the broader galaxy population, the role of mergers in driving nuclear starbursts, and the interplay between galaxy evolution, nuclear activity, and the observed sequence

This study focuses on action recognition in R-BERT, particularly under restricted data and low-light conditions. To enhance action recognition, our approach incorporates delta sampling in the R-BERT framework. Initially, we employ delta sampling to reduce noise in the training dataset by selectively excluding data with significant intensity variations from the training set. Subsequently, we apply delta transformation to enhance training with underexposed images by transforming overexposed images into underexposed ones. Notably, this transformation maintains the original class labels, thereby preventing label fluctuations during the transformation. Consequently, our method yields improved action recognition performance compared to existing techniques in multiple datasets under restricted data and low-light conditions. Experimental results indicate that our proposed approach achieves superior action recognition accuracy in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in action recognition from underexposed and restricted data. This report outlines the technical details of the Content Addressable Concurrent Processor, a unique hardware component that efficiently searches for specific data within an array by activating all possible computation paths simultaneously. By leveraging content-addressable memory, this processor essentially consolidates the search and calculation functions into a single operation, thereby optimizing performance. We have successfully implemented this processor using a Field Programmable Gate Array and have conducted performance evaluations using real-world mathematical applications. Our results show that the CACP outperforms conventional hardware by as much as 17 times for specific problems, and we discuss the potential of this technology to transform the way we design computational systems. Due to the intricate design of the CACP, our development process was hindered by limitations in available CAD tools, and we have identified areas where improvements in VLSI design support could yield significant breakthroughs in several areas, including high-speed numerical computations, artificial intelligence, and genetic engineering. We anticipate that the integration of content-addressable concurrent processors into computational systems will become more feasible with advancements in both hardware and software. This study examines the linearized wave equations derived from first principles in relativistic hydrodynamics, specifically within its viscous regime. By comparing the underlying conservation laws of hydrodynamics to their approximate fluid descriptions, we develop a comprehensive linearized theory, including both first and second-order approximations. The resulting wave equations account for four long-wavelength modes in a barotropic fluid and five in a barotropic fluid with entropy variations. Our analysis reveals the existence of damped sound waves in both cases, with the damped frequency determined by the divergence of the fluid's velocity field and the relaxation time of its four-scattering interaction. Furthermore, we find that in a barotropic fluid with entropy variations, there emerges a quasi-isothermal mode whose damping rate is dictated by the fluid's thermal conductivity and the divergence of its velocity field. The full linearized hydrodynamic tensor is provided, enabling numerical solution for the mode's behavior. Our analysis also provides the dispersion relations and damping rates for both barotropic fluid types. Additionally, we demonstrate that our linearized theory aligns with the Knudsen layer analysis, fulfilling the necessary condition $\lambda \gg$1, where $\lambda$ denotes the mean free path. The linearized wave equations are relevant on the scale $\lambda$ and are derived from their nonlinear counterparts through a direct expansion, bypassing the need for the Chapman-Enskog method. This approach ensures that neither the conservation laws nor the fluid's velocity field are approximated, ensuring accurate solutions down to the smallest scales of interest. This study offers a comprehensive linearized theory for relativistic hydrodynamics within the Knudsen layer and provides the underlying equations for numerical hydrodynamics simulations within this layer. Additionally, it highlights the limitations of its validity, indicating that neither this theory nor its simulations can account for particle scattering in the opposite direction. Instead, they should only capture interactions in the same direction, as defined by the fluid's velocity field. In approximation algorithms, problems with general valuations have been the subject of increasing research attention in recent years, with notable advances on several significant problems, including facility location and sparse steepest path. This study builds upon a fundamental result from Iwana and Sadakane (ISSAC 2014), which demonstrated the existence of a PTAS for general valuation functions that can be efficiently minimized under certain sparsity conditions. Our work expands upon this by providing a specific description of sparsely conditionable valuations and developing a polynomial-time approximate solution for general valuation functions meeting these conditions, with an error rate of (1+1/dn)^k for d-dimensional valuations of degree k. Furthermore, our research yields a PTAS for the sparse steepest path problem with general valuations, with an approximate distance of (1+1/dn)^k in d-dimensional space of degree k. The techniques developed in this research can be applied to give a (2k+1)-approximation for the k-sparse minimum-weight path problem with general valuations. Additionally, our work involves an NP-hard proof for the minimum-weight path problem with general valuations for space S^d when k is greater than the Shannon dimension. Lastly, our research can be seen as an extension to previous work by Iwana and Sadakane (ISSAC 2014) on simple sparsity conditions. Our work is now the base for further research into general valuation transportation problems presented at this year's conference. Despite the valuable information that the learned features of these networks could provide, comprising their visual representations and grammatical structures, current methods lack the capability to effectively interpret and communicate this information. As a result, researchers are facing a pressing need to develop methods that can seamlessly transition between learning from these networks, manipulating their parameters, and extracting valuable information from them. To address this challenge, a diverse range of techniques has emerged, such as visualizing the learned features, presenting the network's decision-making process, and translating the semantic meaning of the features into human-language descriptions. We have also discussed the advantages and limitations of each technique as well as the associated challenges, future research directions, and potential applications. Although much research focuses on identifying false news as an image classification problem, producing a comprehensive and accurate false news dataset is a major obstacle. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces a new framework for detecting emergent false news on social media using multimodal information. By leveraging a small sample dataset and a large collection of true news articles, our proposed model, the Multimodal Neural Process Network, combines a false news classification network and a true news classification network to effectively identify false news. These web maps often contain important information and serve as a critical means of communication, thus their visual presentation holds significant importance. In recognition of the universal nature of web mapping technologies, our research and developed solution can be applied across various mapping domains, from local settings to broader geographic contexts. Our anti-aliassing technique has also been made available as an open-source repository for the benefit of the web mapping community. By exploring the underlying principles and the underlying mathematics of line rendering, along with the underlying principles of spatial anti-aliassing, our research can be expanded across other spatial rendering topics, such as the optimization of semi-transparent polygon filling. Furthermore, it highlights the unique contributions of tomographic analysis in providing a detailed, physical understanding of entanglement and synchronization in complex quantum systems. This insight becomes particularly valuable when working with multi-photon states and optical networks, where the average correlation cannot serve as a comprehensive indicator. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. The detection system, however, encountered various interruptions known as glitches that lasted from milliseconds to several seconds and had considerable impacts on the test results. Although the duration of these glitches was often short, their effect on the experiment's findings cannot be disregarded. This study calculates the statistical significance of the test results taking into account the duration and frequency of glitches occurring during data collection. It demonstrates that the typical glitches observed during the experiment would add up to an acceleration deviation of around 2x10^-16 times the acceleration due to gravity, but this variation greatly depends on the specific characteristics of the glitches. As a result, data collected by the Microscope experiment contains useful information about the Equivalence Principle, despite glitches possibly affecting its validity. Further analysis of the Microscope data by researchers suggests a need for a more nuanced understanding of the glitches that occurred during the experiment in order to fully interpret its findings. It is essential to consider different definitions used for identifying glitches in the data and whether they were genuinely random events. If the latter is confirmed, the impact of glitches could be minimized by extending the duration of data collection without the presence of such anomalies. If glitches were not truly random, the test's validity might be called into question and the Microscope experiment would require optimization to effectively overcome its inherent flaws. Furthermore, to further minimize the effect of glitches on the test, researchers suggest incorporating features of glitch detection used by other experiments, such as cross-checking data from dual test mass setups and implementing more sophisticated data processing methods. If implemented, such changes could enhance the sensitivity of the Microscope experiment by a factor of around 100. Ultimately, despite the challenges posed by glitches, the Microscope experiment has contributed positively to the validation of the weak equivalence principle. An alternative is to use a simplified model where the output is a yes-or-no answer to a specific question, without providing detailed information about the reasoning. Yet, even with just this basic information, it's still difficult to obtain the knowledge from the original model. This study demonstrates that it's possible to acquire the original model's knowledge by training a new model on just a few examples, without the new model needing to be exposed to the original model's data. We achieve this by showing that neural network-based models can be transferred even without having access to the original model's input, simply by relying on examples that highlight the original model's decisions. This knowledge transfer occurs across models of different types, such as those trained with different optimizers, on different datasets, with different hyperparameters, and even across different puzzle types. This breakthrough has significant implications, as it makes it possible to easily share knowledge between machine learning models by just sharing their decision-making capabilities. This research is the first of its kind to investigate the zero-shot knowledge transfer phenomenon, and we present it as an important discovery that could facilitate the easier sharing of knowledge between machine learning models. We introduce an open-source framework that allows researchers to easily replicate and extend our knowledge transfer results across different machine learning models, data sets, and challenges. This study's findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of machine learning models, and we anticipate that they will spark further research into the transfer of knowledge between models. This research is an important step towards better understanding how machine learning models can learn from each other, and we believe that it will contribute to the advancement of the broader machine learning community. We hope that our work will inspire other researchers to build upon this study's findings and to explore even more ways to investigate the complex interactions between machine learning models. We anticipate that our research will also be of interest to the machine learning community, given the significant progress that machine learning models have made in recent years across a wide range of competition challenges. This study has significant implications for how machine learning models can be trained and how they can be used in real-world applications. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert knowledge. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach called co-imitation training, where the agent collaborates with multiple self-exploratory agents to accumulate rich experience by mutual imitation. By leveraging multiple independent paths to the optimal policy, the agent finally converges to a better performance. We test this method on multiple complex tasks, including those requiring high exploration costs and find it to be highly effective. Our results show that co-imitation training achieves comparable or even better performance compared to expert demonstration-based imitation learning, with notable savings in demonstration costs. We also analyze the influence of various factors on this method, including the number of independent agents, their individual risk preferences, and the overall number of training steps. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ericyang2018/CoIT. The theoretical and practical implications of this research are relevant to a wide range of multi-agent reinforcement learning applications, including multi-robot collaboration, recommendation systems, and network optimization. In addition, an extended version of this research appears in the journal Autonomous Systems: Science and Engineering, vol. 2, issue 1, 2023 (early view). Additionally, a related issue concerning delayed expert demonstration data appears in the journal Neural Information Processing Systems 2023. For more information on these related issues, please refer to the provided appendices. The total data evidence for these results amounts to roughly 6 million individual steps across 51 unique scenarios. In this study, we examine quasi-finite simple (QFS) regions within Lie algebras that are derived from nilpotent algebras. These QFS regions can be seen as combinations of generalised Gelfand-Tseitan eigenoperators, which are defined by a Lie algebra's Casimir invariants. Our research reveals that any QFS region is characterised by specific properties related to its central invariants, eigenvalues, and semi-simple rank. We also demonstrate that both classical and quantum Hall algebras can be viewed as specific types of QFS derived algebras. Furthermore, we provide a detailed explanation of the derivation process, explaining how these algebras are constructed from nilpotent Lie algebras and demonstrate that they exhibit universal properties. These properties enable us to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the generators and elements of these algebras and their corresponding representations. Our results also reveal that both classical and quantum Hall algebras can be expressed as closed subalgebras within the universal QFS derived algebras, derived from 2-step nilpotent Lie algebras, providing a unified framework for their study. Additionally, we explore how both classical and quantum Hall algebras can be obtained from nilpotent Lie algebras and discuss their connection to the theory of integrable systems. Our research also identifies new finite-dimensional algebras, derived from step-three nilpotent Lie algebras, that possess both su(3) symmetry and four-dimensional semi-simple rank, providing a unified framework for their study. These new algebras can be seen as generalisations of both classical and quantum Hall algebras and are expected to have applications in the study of quantum physics, in particular in the description of quantum Hall effects that exhibit su(3) symmetry and 5-fold degeneracy. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for parallel document updates through its "findAndModify" method, implementing a variant of transactional coherence known as "sessionless atomicity".  To facilitate formal verification, we have created a formal model of the findAndModify operation, incorporating sessionless atomicity, and then proved that it enforces transactional coherence under specific conditions.  Furthermore, we applied this model to prove that the transactional coherence properties hold for certain configurations of MongoDB, specifically verifying that its findAndModify method maintains atomicity, isolation, and consistency in certain scenarios.  This verification also reveals a previously unreported issue with MongoDB's implementation.  Our validation strategy also serves as a framework for database designers to demonstrate that their implementations meet transactional coherence requirements.  Our verification was carried out and confirmed with the help of the Coq proof assistant.  We also examine how our verification approach can be extended to handle other concurrent operations, such as the "insert" and "remove" methods, and discuss the implications of our findings for the design of concurrent databases.  This verification has been incorporated into a forthcoming textbook on verification.  A previously unreported bug in MongoDB's code was identified as a result of this verification process.  The code for this bug has since been corrected by the MongoDB development team.  Although this bug was subsequently fixed, it was discovered through the verification process that it had been latent for over ten years.  Despite the advances made through this verification, there are still several issues with the transactional coherence of MongoDB's implementation that require further investigation. We present the findings of a nuclear forward scattering study on Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ at elevated pressures, which reveals that this material exhibits ferromagnetic behavior under pressure, in contrast to its room-temperature orthoferrite structure where it displays antiferromagnetic properties. Our study finds that an external pressure of around 18 GPa is required to induce the ferromagnetic state. This phenomenon can also be achieved chemically through doping with copper at a concentration of 12%, also resulting in a ferromagnetic ground state from an initially antiferromagnetic state. Our results suggest that both pressure and copper doping disrupt the long-range magnetic ordering within the Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ structure, leading to the emergence of a ferromagnetic state. This research was conducted at the High-Pressure Beamline of the ESRF, with data collected over the full spectral range and at multiple angles with respect to the scattering vector. This technique provides an in situ and real-time non-destructive analysis of the material's magnetic state. We compare our results to previous research utilizing other methods, including SQUID magnetometry and X-ray diffraction, and find that the material's structural and magnetic properties are consistent across these techniques. We offer possible explanations for the material's magnetic behavior based on its structural composition, including the role of Bi$^{3+}$ cations within the Bi$_5$O$_6$ layer, and suggest future research directions, including investigations into the material's magnetic state at extreme pressures and temperatures. This study showcases the capabilities of nuclear forward scattering to study the magnetic and structural properties of materials under various conditions. We outline the technical specifications of this technique, including the detection system and data collection methodology, and highlight its unique advantages over other methods, such as the ability to collect data simultaneously across multiple angles and spectral ranges. This research provides new insights into the material Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ and demonstrates the effectiveness of nuclear forward scattering as a means of studying the magnetic and structural properties of materials under external pressures. We anticipate that this technique will be valuable in investigating the structural and magnetic behavior of other materials under pressure. The development of cutting-edge laser technology necessitates in-depth understanding of full laser systems, encompassing diode pumps, solid-state lasers, and beam delivery components. This knowledge enables the optimization of system performance, efficiency, and overall operation. However, the intricate nature and diverse origins of these systems pose significant challenges to their reverse engineering, hindrance to the advancement of laser technology through the recovery of obsolete technology. A case study is presented on the enhancement and reverse engineering of a 100 W average power, CPRT (continuously operating, high-power, red-light system) laser used in two-photon microscopy. The original CPRT system featured a complex design with multiple unknown components, which hindered its modification into a green-light system through simple diode-pumped solid-state laser principles. As a result, the need arose to re-engineer the entire system to accommodate a range of output wavelengths. This case study illustrates the intricacies involved in recovering the design of an complex solid-state laser system, highlighting the difficulties encountered and the lessons learned through this experience. The enhanced description of the modified CPRT system, now capable of delivering 2 W of red or green light, serves as an accessible educational resource for the broader scientific community on the intricacies of high-power laser engineering. The recovered design also provides valuable insights for the development of advanced laser technology through the recovery of legacy technology. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the practical utility of reverse engineering high-power laser technology for biological applications, such as two-photon microscopy, by highlighting the significance of system flexibility in output wavelength. The challenge posed by the complexity of these systems also serves as an impetus for the development of open-access educational resources on the inner workings of high-power laser technology. As such, this study contributes to the establishment of an educational platform on the recovery of legacy technology for two-photon microscopy. This platform aims to provide straightforward explanations on the intricacies of high-power laser engineering and to facilitate the recovery of outdated technology to address the technological advancements in microscopy. Given a fixed $p$ with $0 < p \leq 2$, we define an $\ell_p$ space and investigate the behavior of bi-Lipschitz mappings $f$ from subsets of $\ell_p$ to $\ell_p$. Specifically, we explore the properties of bi-Lipschitz mappings $f$ on incompressible subsets $A$ within $\ell_p$, with the goal of determining the minimal increase required for these mappings to be isometric. Our findings reveal that any bi-Lipschitz mapping $f$ from an incompressible subset $A$ within $\ell_p$ must exhibit a significant increase of at least $2^{d-1}$ in its Lipschitz constant, with $d$ representing the dimension of $A$ in cases where $1\le p<2$. However, we demonstrate that this increase is not necessarily achieved by isometric mappings. Moreover, our research establishes that in the scenario where $0 < p < 1$, dimension decrease is evident, with the dimension of $A$ reducing to $d-\lfloor p\log_2(d-1)\rfloor$ for any given $d\ge (1/p)-1$. Conversely, we prove that this dimension decrease is minimal, with $d$ being the smallest possible increase for a bi-Lipschitz mapping from $\ell_p$. Finally, our work also facilitates the extension of these results to Schauder spaces and provides an alternative, more concise proof of previously established results pertaining to the dimension decrease of bi-Lipschitz mappings from incompressible subsets within $\ell_p$ spaces. With these findings, we are able to address and resolve questions posed by Kalton in the field of Banach space theory. Our research is a continuation of prior work conducted by the authors with G. Godefroy and D. Kalton.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology. Researchers use simulations of microwave background experiments to understand the underlying processes that shape anisotropy patterns and facilitate accurate parameter estimation. However, such simulations typically overlook the complex instrumental limitations of real experiments, which can significantly impact their ability to recover true parameters. To address this, we have developed a comprehensive Python package called s4cmb that simulates two-dimensional microwave background maps and associated data sets, incorporating a wide range of instrumental limitations, cosmic microwave background processes, and contamination effects. This versatile tool allows users to explore the complex interplay between real instrumental limitations and microwave background processes that affect parameter estimation. By examining how instrumental limitations impact recovery accuracy, s4cmb can facilitate the optimization of real experiments, such as future CMB-S4-like surveys, by identifying the most critical limitations that need to be addressed through enhanced data collection or instrumental improvements. As such, s4cmb is an invaluable resource for researchers involved in the design, analysis, and interpretation of real microwave background experiments. Furthermore, its code is highly modular and easily extensible, making it suitable for integrating with other research tools. Additionally, we have employed s4cmb to investigate how the recovery accuracy of physical parameters is affected by real instrumental limitations in the context of future CMB experiments, specifically in regards to four distinct scenarios, namely: (1) the current generation of balloon-borne experiments, (2) ground-based experiments with semi-high-resolution channels, (3) the next generation of balloon-borne experiments, and (3) CMB-S4-like experiments. The results obtained with s4cmb provide valuable insights to guide the design of future real experiments and highlight the importance of taking instrumental limitations into consideration when interpreting data sets. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection approach, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed framework, comprising two parallel streams, extracts feature sets from both the spatial domain of images and the frequency domain of discrete cosine transforms. These feature sets are then equally contributions made from both streams to the network, allowing them to learn a shared, discriminative representation for a multi-domain cross-stitch pattern. Through extensive experimentation on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark, our approach demonstrates superior performance, achieving a high accuracy of 82.3% for image classification and 73.5% for video classification, outperforming existing methods while requiring a relatively low parameter count of approximately 0.56 million. Furthermore, the network's efficiency in resource allocation allows for real-time processing on a single GPU. The implementation of the proposed approach shows great potential in the detection of deepfake videos, with results indicating a 6.5% improvement in accuracy when applied to the Celeb-DF-DVD benchmark. The source code for the MD-CSDNetwork has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. Through extensive experimentation and analysis, the detection capabilities of the proposed framework are evaluated and the results are visualized through heatmaps and feature visualization techniques, providing valuable insights into the frequency spectrum-based detection approach. The research concentrates on the development of a universal deepfake detection technique for image and video media, with the aim of overcoming the limitations of previous methods that relied on creating multiple protocol-specific models. The innovative frequency spectrum-based detection approach opens up new research directions in the field, with the potential for the extension of the proposed framework to the detection of additional media types. We address the challenge of robustness to data disruptions by proposing a new distributionally robust decentralized optimization method, DR-DSGD, that minimizes the impact of disruptions in graph-structured data sets. We mathematically frame distribution diversity as a regularized empirical risk minimization problem and leverage it to create a robust proxy problem. Utilizing convexification techniques and conditional gradient methods, we develop an efficient and feasible DR-DSGD algorithm that minimizes the disruption-sensitive loss by optimizing a regularized subproblem. We provide theoretical convergence rate guarantees for DR-DSGD and validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, revealing its superior performance compared to non-disruption-sensitive decentralized methods. Notably, DR-DSGD achieves comparable performance to full-centralized and decentralized approaches while offering substantial improvements in efficiency and data efficiency. Furthermore, DR-DSGD exhibits flexibility in optimizing non-strongly convex objectives and robustness to various graph topologies and node dropout. Thousands of white and blue-white stars in the Milky Way emit near-ultraviolet radiation at intensities that could pose a threat to life on planets orbiting these stars.  To better understand how life on such planets is affected, researchers use spectroscopic data to analyze the ultraviolet output of stars.  However, data on the highest energy ultraviolet spectrum is limited due to the Earth's atmosphere interfering with telescope measurements.  Additionally, simulated stellar flare spectra often overestimate the radiation emitted during the strongest parts of the flare, making it difficult to model how the star's surface behaves during the flare.  This study takes a unique approach to modeling the ultraviolet output of a solar-like star by using data on the star's optical spectrum during a flare.  The approach involves separating the star's optical spectrum into the parts that contribute to the near-ultraviolet continuum and those that do not, and then matching the simulated spectrum to the actual data.  The model then predicts the near-ultraviolet continuum based on the part of the spectrum that controls it, rather than the entire spectrum.  The approach led to a more accurate model of the near-ultraviolet continuum during a flare on the star AD Leo, with an accuracy of 6.5 times better than previous models.  The model also accounts for the effects of the star's magnetic field on the radiation emitted during the flare, and predicts that the near-ultraviolet continuum during the flare will match the predictions of other models, such as the LL-OPTIMIST model, but with a higher energy level.  The approach and model can be applied to other stars, such as K and M stars, by adjusting the model to match the star's optical spectrum during a flare. We investigate the fundamental behavior and performance of Boolean systems with sparsely interconnected nodes that interact with each other and themselves. The systems, characterized by a sparse graph $G$ defining their connections and an independent and identically distributed random variable $X$, follow an uniform distribution over all possible states. A detailed examination of the system's dynamics is conducted under the condition that the graph $G$ is highly interconnected and random variables $X$ are independent of each other. The study focuses on the hybrid state where some nodes have the value 0 and others have the value 1. It is proven that the fraction of nodes with the value 1, denoted as $m_t$, follows an exponential distribution with a rate of 2 under natural updating rules, including majority voting and specifically for the variable $X$, where $E[X^2]=1$. It is also shown that the expected value of any node $Y_t$ at time $t$ is equal to $m_t$ and does not depend on the initial state. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the majority voting rule has the same behavior as the variable $X$ when $E[X^2]=1$. The results are validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulations. The findings have implications for the recent study on the evolution of networks in online social media platforms, published in the journal Management Science, which assumed that systems with self-interactions and multi-node connections behave similarly to systems with independent and identically distributed components. In this research, we examine medium access control (MAC) techniques for a radar network that utilizes frequency-modulation continuous wave (FMCW) technology. Our analysis reveals that traditional CSMA and slotted ALOHA approaches have limitations in radar systems due to the long duration of their sweep periods. We demonstrate that a modified ALOHA system, where nodes can transmit at intervals shorter than their sweep times, offers better performance. We then analyze the packet collision rate for this ALOHA variant and propose an adaptive transmission strategy that optimizes ALOHA performance by tuning access probability in relation to node density. Our findings show that this strategy yields significant improvements in data transfer efficiency and can be further refined by considering key parameters of FMCW radar systems. Notably, we find that the optimal access probability is directly proportional to the square of the ratio of sweep time to transmission duration. This optimal strategy can be implemented with minimal overhead, and our results are validated through simulations up to 10 million data packets. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that employs HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-driven generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts serve as meta-learned representations that transform input tokens into task-relevant features, enabling our model to tackle diverse tasks by generating appropriate hyper-prompts. By optimizing hyper-prompts via a task-specific loss function, our model can effectively solve classification, sequence-to-sequence, and few-shot learning tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt demonstrates exceptional performance when there is a scarcity of labeled data for the target task, thanks to its ability to extract task-relevant information from input data automatically. By decentralizing task information within hyper-prompts, HyperPrompt facilitates a more flexible and efficient hyper-parameter optimization process, outperforming several prominent prompt-based baseline models. Moreover, our model showcases impressive generalization capabilities in multi-task learning and T5-like pre-training scenarios. The source code of HyperPrompt is publicly available at https://github.com/THU-OGS/HyperPrompt.

In numerical relativity, the BSSN formulation is commonly employed to solve the Einstein field equations. However, this formulation is incomplete without additional constraints, specifically the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, which must be satisfied to ensure physical validity of the solutions. We present a novel method, called Conformal Transverse-Tangential decomposition (CTTK), for solving the momentum constraints. This approach modifies the standard TT-decomposition used in conformal field theory, introducing a decomposition of the second-order momentum constraints into a conformal part and a transverse-tangential part. We leverage this decomposition to solve the momentum constraints, first solving the conformal part using an iterative finite-difference method and then employing the solution to solve the transverse-tangental part. The resulting method is highly efficient and flexible, enabling the use of a wide range of potential conformal metric decompositions, including both conformally flat and non-flat decompositions. We showcase the effectiveness of CTTK by applying it to a complex binary black hole merger simulation, demonstrating its ability to produce physically realistic results. The method exhibits particular advantages when employed with non-conformally flat decompositions, which we also examine in detail. The method's source code is an independent contribution to the Einstein Toolkit numerical relativity framework. The technique's potential applications extend to multiple related areas, including numerical cosmology and the study of black hole formation. The method's code is built using the Cactus framework and specific additions to the Einstein Toolkit. The method's performance is assessed against traditional multigrid solvers, revealing CTTK's efficiency and flexibility, especially with non-conformally flat decompositions. The method's impact on numerical solutions is examined through convergence studies, demonstrating that CTTK's solutions align with theoretical predictions, albeit with reduced convergence rates. The method's potential future improvements include optimizing its performance for multiple processors and further investigation of its applicability to numerical cosmology. The method's unique features provide a foundation for exploring a broader range of conformal decompositions, potentially leading to breakthroughs in numerical relativity. The method's code is available through public repositories, including the Einstein Toolkit's GitHub page, under permissive licenses that facilitate open collaboration and contribution. This work examines the effects of temperature anisotropy on geodesic acoustic modes (GAMs) in the edge plasma of tokamaks, focusing on the impact on their propagation and growth rates. Linearized fluid theory was utilized to investigate the anisotropy's effect under oblique propagation angles, revealing significant increases in GAM growth rates by up to three times their anisotropy-independent values, alongside enhanced rates of phase propagation. A link between temperature anisotropy and electron flow anisotropy was identified, suggesting that electron flow anisotropy could drive GAM growth in scenarios where electron temperature anisotropy is minimal. Numerical simulations based on data from the TEXTOR tokamak experiment demonstrated that temperature anisotropy can cause the frequency of GAMs to deviate from its anisotropy-independent value, potentially making it a diagnostic tool for measuring temperature anisotropy. The anisotropy's effect on GAMs was found to be influenced by the flow anisotropy-eigenvalue relationship, resulting in specific frequency, propagation, and growth rate patterns for different anisotropy levels. The study further reveals that temperature anisotropy can lead to the sideband formation of GAMs, offering an anisotropy-related explanation for the observed broad frequency spectra in tokamak edge plasma, as well as the relationship between plasma frequency, anisotropy, and the flow anisotropy-eigenvalue relationship. The work presented provides theoretical foundations for experimentally verifying the impact of temperature anisotropy on GAMs using next-generation multidimensional diagnostic tools, such as high-speed cameras and advanced interferometry systems, to further understand the anisotropy's effect on GAMs and their relation to electron flow anisotropy. The study also highlights the potential for temperature anisotropy to drive major plasma phenomena, such as electron flow anisotropy, ion cyclotron restriking, and geodesic acoustic mode generation, offering a statistical analysis of the anisotropy's effect based on the flow anisotropy-eigenvalue relationship, as well as a review of the underlying plasma physics and the relationship between temperature anisotropy and electron flow anisotropy. The work presented is relevant to the current research in the field of plasma physics, particularly in the understanding of plasma phenomena in magnetic confinement devices, such as tokamaks, as well as in the study of plasma behavior in the solar tachocline and in magnetic fields within stars

Revisiting the quantum annealing process through a variational principle approach, we find that most near-optimally sampled instances in Ising spin glasses are actually trapped in local minima with energy values close to the solution energy. This phenomenon occurs because the quantum annealing Hamiltonian has a mix of ferromagnetic and anti-ferromagnetic interactions that cause trapped samples to have a mixture of stoquastic and non-stoquastic components. When quantum fluctuations are present, decoherence from spin coherence or laser heating can resolve this issue by transforming the non-stoquastic part of the Hamiltonian, resulting in an avoided crossing in the energy spectrum and enabling the escape from local minima. We also observe that randomly modifying the quantum annealing Hamiltonian can lead to successful, although much less likely, escapes from local minima. Lastly, we find that an overdrive of the annealing process also increases the probability of escaping local minima, but this comes at the cost of reduced solution accuracy. Ultimately, our findings suggest that quantum annealing is inherently prone to failure, implying that its effectiveness relies heavily on the specific characteristics of the Hamiltonian used. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of examining the entire energy landscape of an Ising spin glass to gain a deeper understanding of quantum annealing's behavior. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s World Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. As a result of these difficulties, the lab operated with a minimal staff, relying heavily on external resources and taking an approach that emphasized modest, manageable projects over more ambitious goals. Despite these limitations, the lab made notable contributions, particularly in the fields of astrophysics, with van Rhijn at the forefront. His leadership oversaw the development of the Harvard Annals, a catalog of 1,643 stars with precise radial velocity measurements, as well as several subgroups of the Selected Areas. Upon his retirement in 1957, van Rhijn passed the direction of the lab to its new head, Lodewijk Woltjer, marking the end of his nearly 36-year tenure. The rising computational demands in modern deep neural networks necessitate the use of distributed learning techniques, involving multiple machines processing different data regions to train the models. However, the cost is typically doubled due to the need for synchronized models and devices. This paper introduces an innovative approach called regional critic training, allowing each machine to maintain its unique parameters and updating the model in an asynchronous manner. Experimental results show that regional critic training achieves significant efficiency gains, with speedups of 1.6 to 3.1 times when using 64 machines for various benchmark datasets and models. Furthermore, our method reduces memory usage by half, making it an effective solution for large-scale deep learning. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate an in-depth exploration of phylogenetic networks, various methods for generating them have been developed and studied in the field of computational biology. Recent research has demonstrated the utility of comparing generated networks to actual phylogenetic networks, employing metrics such as network size and tree density. However, the field lacks a systematic comparison of the structural properties of phylogenetic network generators themselves. This study addresses this gap by systematically comparing the structural properties of a range of phylogenetic network generators, including Ashkelon networks, Reticulate Networks, Breakpoint networks, and others, using a variety of analysis tools such as graph centrality measures, clustering coefficient calculations, and community detection algorithms. Our research explores how these structural properties impact the performance of these generators in producing accurate mini-gene families and examines the relationship between the generators' properties and their parameter settings. Our findings reveal that different centrality measures yield inconsistent results, exhibit varying responsiveness to parameter adjustments, and sometimes fail to capture the inherent characteristics of these networks. On the other hand, community structures and clustering coefficients prove more reliable indicators of a network's quality. Interestingly, some networks exhibit community structures that mirror those of the input tree, whereas others do not. Our work provides a comprehensive evaluation of the structural properties of phylogenetic network generators and highlights their diversity, offering valuable insights for the bioinformatics community on the importance of transparent code and open data practices. Furthermore, our research emphasizes the necessity for a critical examination of the underlying design of these generators in relation to the actual properties of phylogenetic networks. Ultimately, this study provides a foundation for further exploration of the intricate relationships between the structure of phylogenetic network generators, generated networks, and actual phylogenetic networks. In addition, it highlights the value of interdisciplinary research for the computational biology community, as well as the NoyMirror method for comparing network structures. We examine topological and localization properties in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. Our study focuses on the Topological Anderson Insulator, first proposed by Anderson in 1971. We utilize both numerical and analytical methods to investigate the effects of correlated disorders on topological invariants and boundary modes. Our results show that strong spatial correlations in disorders can transfer topological characteristics from the idealized model to the disordered version. However, once the correlation length exceeds the model's lattice scale, the impact of correlation is minimized, revealing a correlation length-dependent topological phase. Furthermore, we found that strong disorders can induce the topological Anderson phase in model parameters that would not normally exhibit topological behavior. Conversely, in cases that would normally exhibit topological behavior, strong disorders can instead create nongapped phases at zero energy. The boundary modes' localization properties are influenced by the disorder strength and correlation length, resulting in various scenarios, including the localization of boundary modes in the topological phase. In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the generation of the Higgs mass matrix is intricately linked to the breakdown of electroweak symmetry. This process involves complex, higher-dimensional couplings which ultimately result in a physical, real Higgs mass matrix. The associated residual CP-violating phases within the Higgs sector stem directly from the underlying new physics. Consequently, the characteristics of the physical Higgs bosons, including their masses, mixing angles, and CP properties, serve as indirect probes of the complex parameters of the underlying theory. This connection between the complex parameters of the MSSM and the physical properties of the Higgs bosons provides a precise framework for confronting the MSSM with experimental data related to the Higgs sector. This review offers a comprehensive overview of the CP properties of the Higgs bosons as derived from the underlying physics of the MSSM, encompassing a detailed analysis of the contributions of the top-quark, stop-squark, and their associated loops, alongside an examination of the impact of complex strong gauge and soft supersymmetry-breaking terms. This review is concluded with a thorough examination of the present and anticipated constraints on the complex parameters of the MSSM as derived from experimental data on the Higgs sector. This analysis is complemented by a detailed overview of the underlying physics of the MSSM, making this review an exhaustive resource on the phenomenology of the CP properties of the Higgs bosons within the MSSM. The intricate relationship between the complex parameters of the MSSM and the physical characteristics of the Higgs bosons has a direct bearing on the ability to accurately determine the underlying parameters of the theory. This consideration assumes a critical role in full exploitation of experimental data related to the Higgs sector, as it is heavily dependent on the complex parameters of the underlying theory. We examine the issue of linearity testing in a network autoregressive model, where we assess whether the model's non-linear components contain significant information that aids in forecasting. By comparing the coefficients of a linear version of the model to zero, we develop a suitable testing framework that incorporates a Monte Carlo method and controls the family-wise error rate. Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of our proposed test by conducting extensive simulation studies, and intriguingly find that it outperforms alternative approaches under certain conditions. Additionally, we apply and illustrate the practical utility of our method through a substantial real-world data analysis example involving macroeconomic variables. Interestingly, our results reveal intriguing patterns where the proposed test exhibits both superior and inferior performance compared to other methods for specific non-linear configurations. We complement our findings by obtaining a quantitative evaluation of our test's performance, and find that it achieves a notable success rate of approximately 40% in simulation settings. We make available the code for our simulation studies and real-world analysis under an open-source framework. Additionally, we provide a preliminary examination of a potential extension to our method involving the identification of specific linear sub-models. Nonetheless, a notable limitation of our research is the lack of a explicit asymptotic distribution for the test statistic. We do, however, offer a theoretical justification for controlling the family-wise error rate. Finally, we explore potential future research directions for our method, and highlight potential avenues for investigation, such as the exclusive assessment of linear components, the exclusive assessment of non-linear components, and the assessment of components in models with time-varying parameters. Ultimately, we contend that testing linearity in network autoregressive models provides valuable insights that can enhance our understanding of model performance and forecasting accuracy. Additionally, we acknowledge the expertise and guidance provided by Dr. Ruijun Wang in the development of our research. In addition, we express our gratitude to the anonymous referees for their constructive feedback and suggestions. In conclusion, we reiterate the complexity inherent in testing linear components in network autoregressive models, and the need for further research in this area. In essence, our research represents a pioneering effort in this field, and we anticipate that future studies will build upon and expand our findings. In fact, we anticipate that future studies will investigate alternative testing methods, such as the Hansen-Hodrick test, the J-test, the Koenker test, and the local linear kernel test, among others. In fact, we expect that future studies will explore new directions in this area, and we look forward to learning from their findings.

Quantum states of light in multiple cavities hold great promise for breaking through the photon counting barrier in metrology, offering a possible path to extremely precise measurements. Research has primarily focused on one-cavity configurations, leaving the study of multi-cavity systems under strong coupling conditions largely unexplored. In our study, we examine a two-cavity network with strong coupling, where the interaction between light states in the separate cavities is intensified by large, overlapping spontaneous emission fields. Using a novel model that incorporates the effects of beam splitting and vacuum field dressing, we identified a regime in which the most informative states about an unknown phase shift are entangled states between the two cavities. Under these conditions, the most precise measurements for certain quantities can surpass the standard quantum limit by a factor of four. Furthermore, we demonstrate the realizability of such states and the achievement of optimal metrological performance through controlled application of strong coupling in two-cavity configurations. These variations can result in changes to the network's structural characteristics, such as its small-world properties, which may not be accounted for by the average bandwidth available to a VM.  To gauge the potential impact of these changes on application performance, we introduce a framework for assessing scalability that takes into consideration both the variability of network deployments and the limitations of VMs.  Through the use of open-source network prototypes and stress testing, we demonstrate the significant effects that changes in network structure can have on application scalability and speed.  Our research can serve as a reference for designers of cloud systems who need to deploy applications that require high levels of scalability and speed.  We also introduce a new concept called "application efficiency variance," which measures the impact of variations in network structure on scalability, and provide a scorecard that can be used to gauge this variance for different applications.  We find that Hadoop exhibits a high variance in efficiency when deployed on networks with varying levels of noise, but it maintains good scalability with high probability, whereas Redis exhibits a low variance in efficiency but has low scalability in some cases.  Furthermore, we find that the variance in efficiency is influenced by the degree of fault tolerance incorporated into an application, with higher levels of fault tolerance resulting in increased variance.  We also find that the efficiency variance of an application can be mitigated to some extent by increasing the number of VMs used in the stress test, but this has a limited effect. Contextual linear bandits is an important model for personalization in online learning, where agents make decisions for individual users based on their context. We investigate a new, more challenging setting where agents must learn from feedback in a connected network, without observing context or payoff information, and must also make decisions for their own users. For this setting, we develop a distributed learning algorithm that achieves an almost square-root payoff improvement over time, and analyze its performance in various network configurations. Notably, our results show that allowing communication among agents can lead to significantly better learning rates. We also present a lower bound indicating that our algorithm's payoff improvement is near-optimal. Finally, we apply our model to a contextual newsvendor problem and devise an efficient, decentralized solution. This model is relevant to various areas, including healthcare, ride-sharing, and online advertising, and could help address issues of scale in modern online learning systems.
