Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a dual-case study design, combining both qualitative and quantitative approaches. Twenty-seven respondents from two Scrum project cases participated in in-depth interviews. A survey of 206 Scrum team members was also conducted. Our findings indicate that home working has a negative impact on Scrum's success factors, including clear goals, effective communication, and collective responsibility. Moreover, our data reveals the challenges of home working, such as decreased active commitment, reduced informal interaction, and difficulties with virtual trust-building. Based on these insights, we provide practical recommendations for practitioners and potential areas for future research. This study's results can provide valuable insights for companies operating remote Scrum projects. This study's objective is to investigate the influence of home working on the success of Scrum projects. Background and Related Work Home working, also known as remote working or teleworking, involves working from a remote location using communication technology to collaborate with colleagues. This work arrangement offers employees flexibility in their working life, with potential benefits for companies, including increased employee satisfaction, lower turnover rates, and cost savings. However, home working can also present several challenges for team members, including difficulties with communication, trust-building, and building strong working relationships. Scrum is an agile framework that facilitates collaboration within cross-functional teams, helping them respond to changing requirements and deliver working products. A Scrum project consists of several key phases, including planning, development, and review phases. Success factors for Scrum projects include clear goals, effective communication, and collective responsibility. Methodology This study combines both qualitative and quantitative approaches to explore the influence of home working on the success of Scrum projects. Two case studies were selected from a survey of 206 Scrum team members, with the participants working from home due to the COVID-19 pandemic. In-depth interviews were conducted with twenty-seven respondents from these two case studies. A survey of 206 Scrum team members was also conducted to validate the results. Our research manipulates event shapes in a more nuanced way to better understand how elliptical flow is created in heavy ion collisions. By sorting events based on the alignment of their long and short axes, we observe that elliptical flow is largely produced by interactions occurring in both directions. However, the magnitude of the effect varies with transverse momentum. Once transverse momentum exceeds a certain threshold, the influence of the medium on charged particles as they travel in the direction of the event's short axis becomes less significant than their initial momentum. This is reflected in the increasing gap between in-plane and out-of-plane spectra as transverse momentum increases. By taking this multi-dimensional approach, our study offers a more intricate understanding of heavy ion collisions and elliptical flow. The relationship between event shapes, spectra, and elliptical flow is further illustrated by a new method that calculates flow coefficients based on event shape manipulation. The results of this study, coupled with existing research on flow anisotropy, provide a comprehensive view of heavy ion collisions and elliptical flow. It is also demonstrated that the manipulation of event shapes can be used as a reference to determine the influence of the medium on charged particles as they travel through the hot, dense nuclear medium. This influence, expressed as elliptical flow elasticity, is found to be relatively constant across different transverse momentum thresholds. Notably, the same elasticity values are obtained when elliptical flow is calculated using a systematic or logarithmic method, further confirming the validity of event shape manipulation. However, when considering only semi-central and central collisions, a slight variation in elasticity is observed, with a slight decrease as collision centrality decreases. This study is based on data collected by the ALICE at the Large Hadron Collider. It is essential to reproduce these results with an upgraded detector to verify the validity of event shape manipulation across various experimental platforms. It is also crucial to incorporate flow proton-proton collision data into this study to better comprehend the creation of elliptical flow in minimum bias collisions and understand how it relates to heavy ion collisions. Building on existing research, our study demonstrates that event shape manipulation is a precise tool for analyzing elliptical flow and provides a new perspective on heavy ion collisions, elliptical flow, and the hot, dense nuclear medium created in these events. It is also shown that event shape manipulation is a robust, collision-energy-independent method. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of further research on proton-proton collisions to comprehend the creation of elliptical flow and the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. This paper investigates the extreme goodput performance gain of optimal power control over binary power control in interference networks with $K$ users, and we show the gain rises at a rate of approximately $\sqrt{K}$ as the number of users increases. To achieve this, we first establish a binary power control network with a similar throughput performance to optimal power control networks in the high interference regime for any number of users. Consequently, the maximum separation between the goodput performance of optimal and binary power control strategies in favor of optimal power control is directly determined by the ratio of the areas under their respective capacity functions, and this ratio is precisely quantified as $\sqrt{K}$ in the high interference regime. Notably, this gain does not come without a cost, as the energy consumption of optimal power control is proportional to $K$, in contrast to binary power control which only requires a logarithmic increase in energy. As such, optimal power control may offer significant advantages in areas like energy harvesting and cellular networks. As a side effect of our findings, we also derive a novel, closed-form expression for the extremal goodput performance gain in networks with any number of users. Finally, a binary power control strategy that achieves the same throughput performance as optimal power control in the high interference regime can be applied across a broad range of interference networks, including those with asymmetric link capacities, two-way channels, and $K$ user multiple-access channels. Ultimately, this research provides a fundamental understanding of the extreme goodput performance gain of optimal power control over binary power control in interference networks with any number of users. Additionally, we offer a theoretical framework that can be used to analyze and compare the goodput performance of different transmission strategies in interference networks. This framework can be particularly useful for tackling complex problems in the high interference regime. In the high interference regime, the optimal transmission strategy in interference networks with any number of users involves a binary power control approach that forms multiple distinct classes of active users, each with their own unique transmission strategy. The size of these classes holds significant theoretical and practical significance, as they directly impact the throughput performance of optimal power control in interference networks. In this paper, we examine a versatile meson form factor formula that incorporates both linear and logarithmic functions of the spacelike momentum transfer. This investigation is significant because it offers a uniform framework that can predict the electromagnetic form factors of mesons with different quark configurations. Furthermore, we determine the parameters of this form factor formula for several mesons using a linear combination of their spectral functions, as derived from lattice QCD data. Our results demonstrate that this uniform form factor formula accurately captures the electromagnetic properties of mesons with both quark-antiquark and quark-quark interactions. Additionally, we observe that the spectral functions of mesons with quark-quark interactions exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to their quark-antiquark counterparts. This distinction highlights the importance of considering the nature of the meson's quark content when analyzing its electromagnetic form factor. We also explore potential applications of this uniform form factor framework to the weak transition form factors of mesons. Nonetheless, more precise lattice QCD data or Monte Carlo calculations within the context of lattice QCD are needed to fully utilize the potential of this uniform form factor framework. In particular, we outline the requirements for investigating the electromagnetic and weak form factors of $D$ and $\Sigma_c$ mesons as well as vector mesons within this unified scheme. This uniform form factor formula can also be relevant to the study of hadron structure within the context of chiral effective models, such as the hidden local symmetry theory, particularly when considering the electromagnetic form factors of composite hadrons. Ultimately, this investigation contributes to our understanding of hadron structure and may provide valuable insights into the behavior of hadrons when they interact with electromagnetic or weak forces. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering the impact of negation on meaning. Although negation is a fundamental aspect of language, having an impact on all other elements such as affirmation, quantity, quality, possibility, and necessity, there is a significant lack of attention to negation in RACE-type comprehension tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce CONDAQA, a diverse Chinese comprehension dataset that requires reasoning in the presence of negation. It comprises 10,368 human-written questions concerning the reasoning required to understand negated text. Our data showcases various negation-based comprehension scenarios including but not limited to, negating affirmations, quantifiers, and quality descriptors. exactly localized states of particles that have been separated from their initial
location and we show that these states maintain their form over time without any
degradation, even in the presence of strong perturbations. These states can be
easily created using a weak control field and they provide a high signal
amplification of up to 400 times the initial value. Notably, this property of
amplification is not limited to the site where the state is localized, but can be
observed across the entire chain. We discovered that these states possess a
self-reinforcing effect, where interacting with one particle uses the energy of the
other particles to maintain its own form, leading to a continuous amplification of
the state. This mechanism could potentially be applied to create a self-sustaining
amplification process in discrete quantum systems. Furthermore, we observed that
these states exhibit a phenomenon of mutual reinforcement, where the presence of
one particle causes the amplification of the other, and this could be utilized to
develop a method for enhancing the visibility of odd-even state separations. 
These findings can be experimentally verified using current discrete quantum walk
technologies. 
Notably, these results differ from previous findings, which demonstrated the
amplification of discrete quantum walk states; our discovery, however, involves a
different type of walk, one with a varying walk distance, whereas previous
amplification occurred following extensive walking. 
Our study provides a theoretical explanation for the recent experimental
observations of discrete quantum walk state amplification, and it sheds light on the
discrete differences that distinguish continuous and discrete quantum walk. 
These outcomes also offer a new perspective on the management of discrete quantum
walk states, indicating that their properties can be modified through their walk
history. 
Our research can be applied to the development of discrete quantum walk protocols

separations, and state transformation, as well as to the study of discrete
quantum walk in graph intersections and discrete quantum walk with multiple
coincident peaks.

Our observations with the FAST at a high sensitivity reveal the extended HI distribution around the M101 galaxy, comprising several small nebulae outside its main disk and a protruding HI tail. Unlike previous studies, our data show that these features lie beyond a 50,000 km/s threshold, corresponding to a virial temperature, thereby providing the first direct evidence of HI gas beyond a group of galaxies' gravitational potential influence. A bridge of HI gas spans approximately 75 kpc, connecting M101 to its nearest neighbor NGC 5477. The HI tail of M101 extends up to 175 kpc in length, exhibiting a curved shape and suggesting that its tip may be interacting with the HI gas surrounding NGC 5477. Our findings support the theory that a collision between M101 and NGC 5477 led to the latter's formation, and the HI tail of M101 may be a result of this encounter. Additionally, we find that the HI bridge and tail of M101 hold similarities to a ring-like structure surrounding the galaxy. Our data also reveal an HI tail on the opposite side of M101, thought to be pointing towards the Milky Way, a potential target for future radio observations from Earth. Furthermore, we determine the HI mass of the extra-planar nebulae and tail in M101, along with an estimation of its HI mass-to-dust ratio. Our observations are consistent with previous studies on the structure and composition of M101's HI envelope. Our research provides a more comprehensive understanding of the HI distribution around M101 and its surrounding galaxy group, while our findings also open up avenues for further astrological research. This equation can be expressed as a sum of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^2 = b$, where all coefficients $a_i$ are derived from elements within a global field (such as $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}(X)$, or $\mathbb{F}_q(T)$). Our focus lies on determining whether there exist integer solutions to this equation, given that all coefficients $a_i$ are themselves integers within the global field. We establish that, for a quadratic equation of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^2 = b$, there exists a method to find all possible pairs of $(a_1,\ldots,a_n,b)$ that satisfy the condition of having integer solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method is effective even when the coefficients are subject to constraints. Building on this result, we develop a way to efficiently solve equations of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^2 = b \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i^2$. Allowing for parameters within sums, we can derive solutions for sums of the form $\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}}a_P^2 = \sum_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}}b_Q^2$, provided that all coefficients $a_P$ and $b_Q$ are derived from elements within a global field. Lastly, we explore applications of these techniques to Diophantine equations and algebraic surfaces defined over global fields. Notably, we find all solutions to the equation $\sum_{i=1}^{23}a_i^2 = 67 \cdot \left(\frac{11+3\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2$ within the rational numbers, a problem initially posed by H. Cohen. Additionally, we investigate the number of lattice points with specific distances within the rational plane. Finally, we examine the relationship between our findings and the works of A. Thue, V. J. Kac, and R. M. Garsia. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  This research analyzes the impact of mandatory therapy for convicted individuals on their employment, income, and likelihood of recidivism within the same sector.  Uniquely, access to required treatment is not optional, providing a natural experiment to study treatment effectiveness.  By comparing data before and after the treatment as well as with peers in similar circumstances, the research reveals significant improvements in mental health, reduced likelihood of re-offending, and increased income following the mandated therapy.  Notably, employment rates show a consistent increase across all categories of offenses, suggesting a broader, undisputed benefit of the treatment requirement.  One potential limitation of this research is the absence of direct mental health disorder data, which is compensated for by the unique, non-optimal nature of treatment participation.  Using a broader definition of mental health-related variables does not yield the same results, indicating the importance of scrutinizing data sources and potentially extending this analysis to other segments of the criminal justice system.  The findings suggest that making therapy a necessity for convicted individuals can be an efficient and cost-beneficial means of reducing recidivism and poverty within the criminal justice system. Generalized maximum likelihood estimation is an established method for estimating parameters in models with mixing mechanisms. By extending previous work of Basu et al., we provide generalized maximum likelihood estimators for mixing parameters such as the variance of a normal distribution, the dispersion of a Poisson distribution, or the probability of success in a binomial distribution. We demonstrate the utility of these estimators in developing methods for sampling rare or hard-to-compute quantities, like generating conditional Bernouillies given a large number, or approximating the distribution of the maximum or the median of a normal distribution. We also investigate the properties of these estimators and offer theoretical guarantees on their performance, including asymptotic normality and a rate of convergence. Through simulated data and real-world experiments, we showcase the effectiveness of generalized maximum likelihood estimation in comparison to alternative methods. The technique is also adaptable to accommodate multiple mixing parameters, as shown through the generation of conditional Bernoulli variables given two observations. The R and Python codes for the experiments are available online. The method may also be used to yield improvements in existing algorithms, such as accelerated temporary storage for streaming applications. The technique is currently under consideration for inclusion in the Batcher algorithm, although the rationale for this potential incorporation remains speculative at this point. Membrane rafts are semi-firm combinations of membrane components that have been widely recognized as crucial elements in cell signaling. They are often seen as mobile, roughly 50 nanometer patches that can provide a local platform for protein interactions and molecular transactions. However, recent studies have used advanced techniques to closely examine raft dynamics and protein behavior within them, revealing an unexpected finding - there are significant gaps in the composition of these putative rafts. These voids suggest that the traditional concept of membrane rafts needs revision, and instead, they might be seen as loose assemblages of related proteins that are held together by fluctuating bonds, allowing for a more fluid and dynamic understanding of cellular processes. Furthermore, this research implies that the composition and organization within these aggregates can change over time, which could have important implications for our current knowledge of various cellular phenomena, such as how some proteins are accurately delivered, the efficient transfer of molecules across the membrane, and the initiation of certain cellular processes. Additionally, this study highlights the need to reassess and revise previous models of cellular function in light of these new observations. In this review, we will delve into the methods used to study membrane rafts, the composition of various co-assemblies, and the functional significance of protein binding affinities, as well as the broader implications of these findings for our understanding of cellular biology. A particle can be genuinely nonlocal by itself, as seen in the phenomenon of particle steering, which indicates that the state of one particle is instantly affected by the state of its entangled counterpart, even when they are separated by large distances. This effect overcomes classical communication limitations, which would otherwise allow state updates through, for instance, publicly announcing the chosen basis for measuring one particle, thereby compromising the particle pair's entanglement and nonlocal properties. Furthermore, our study reveals that particle steering is inextricably linked with single-particle entanglement, which can arise from various sources, including the interaction between one particle traveling through an optical fiber and the fiber's electromagnetic field, or the entanglement of one particle with a central system undergoing continuous phase modulation. These scenarios demonstrate that single-particle entanglement is a hallmark of nonlocality and can give rise to a wide range of genuinely nonlocal phenomena. Additionally, we show that particle steering is essential for genuinely nonlocal phenomena, such as particle steering-based beaming and particle steering-based teleportation. Furthermore, we propose the use of particle steering as a means of detecting single-particle entanglement and nonlocality. Finally, we investigate the relationship between particle steering and other nonlocal phenomena, such as particle entanglement, nonlocality in the sense of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox, and superluminal transfer of information, and find that particle steering is more resilient than these phenomena, as it is not affected by the process of state collapse or the choice of measurement basis. Consequently, particle steering is the most dependable indicator of nonlocality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that particle steering can be achieved through single-particle interactions with environments, such as the interaction of a particle with the radiation field of a laser, the interaction of a particle with the spins of atomic ensembles, or the interaction of a particle with the dielectric medium through which it travels. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically on BMOA*p and its analogue $\tilde{\text{BMOA}}^*p$, for $p\in (0, \infty)$. We explore the maximal semigroup of composition operators on BMOA*p and provide a detailed characterization of its members. Moreover, we examine the maximal semigroup of composition operators on $\tilde{\text{BMOA}}^*p$ and provide a characterization of its elements under the assumption that $p=1$. Moreover, this article also delves into the characterization of the maximal semigroup of integral operators on BMOA*p and $\tilde{\text{BMOA}}^*p$. We establish connections between integral operators and composition operators, specifically discussing how certain composition operators can be expressed as integral operators. This article is a continuation of our previous work in [J. Math. Inequal., 2022].

Research output and knowledge growth over time are often analyzed through various indicators such as publication numbers and citation counts. However, there is evidence suggesting that the pace of knowledge production accelerates, yet the gains from this acceleration are not reflected in proportional increases in meaningful knowledge. This study delves deeper by examining high-citation publications in science and engineering fields, focusing on their distribution and growth. It becomes apparent that the majority of knowledge growth originates from a shrinking fast lane composed of rapidly accelerating high-citation papers. Although this fast lane accounts for a minimal percentage of publications, its importance cannot be overemphasized, as it is responsible for a substantial portion of new knowledge. Consequently, attention should be directed at preserving the resources allocated to this section, as well as investing in the underlying fundamental research that supports the fast lane. It is also crucial to monitor the widening gap between the knowledge generated within the fast lane and the rest of the scientific literature. It is recommended to refine productivity metrics by incorporating features such as half-life of citations to better assess the long-term value of fundamental research. Ultimately, preserving the balance between scientific productivity and the amount of knowledge generated requires a deeper understanding of the underlying processes and dynamics at play. It is also essential to acknowledge that reversing the acceleration of knowledge production is not feasible, thus it is crucial to adapt to this shift and the resulting changes in research output. It is essential to redefine research success in terms of the influence it has on the scientific community and the knowledge base as a whole, rather than solely focusing on the quantity of publications. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the current state of scientific productivity and knowledge growth, as well as potential solutions to the emerging disparities, and highlights the value of exploring these concepts through the lens of accelerating processes. Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of viewing research output and knowledge growth through a holistic and dynamic perspective, rather than a static one. This perspective emphasizes the importance of adaptability in the face of changing conditions and the necessity of a community-driven approach to addressing these challenges. This study has implications for various aspects of the scientific community, including funding, employment, and the overall direction it should take in the future. Mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs) rely on external service providers (ASPs) to deliver network access, a trend observed in various countries. In the UK, for example, around 20% of mobile subscribers are MVNO customers, with well-known brands like Giffgifi and Plusnet utilizing the services of several major ASPs such as EE, O2, Three, and Vodafone. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) investigated the MVNO market, concluding that significant barriers existed for new entrants to secure relationships with ASPs, affecting competition and consumer choice. In response, the CMA recommended that ASPs unbundle their portfolios, allowing new MVNOs to acquire services from established providers. However, the effectiveness of this policy depends on the interactions between firms within the market structure. Our model builds upon the CMA's findings, analyzing the decision-making process of both MVNOs and ASPs in a strategic context. We developed a model where multiple MVNOs compete in a Bertrand competition with negative margins, and these firms act as buyers for the mobile access services provided by multiple ASPs operating in a capacity competition. Our model showcases a mixed-equilibrium outcome characterized by price stickiness, where prices are set above the critical level that would result from a perfectly competitive market. Our analysis also indicates that the bundling practices of ASPs contribute to this outcome by creating barriers to entry for new MVNOs. In addition, we discovered that the effect of the CMA's recommended policy, unbundling of services, depends on the firms' entry and exit strategies. Our research provides a theoretical framework for examining the most effective policy design to address the issues faced by new entrants in the MVNO market. Our findings suggest that the greatest entry benefits for new MVNOs could be achieved by implementing a hybrid model, combining elements of the current bundled market structure with the CMA's recommended policy of unbundled services. This model's potential advantages and limitations are illustrated through numerical examples. Our research offers a policy framework that could be applied to other auxiliary service markets that feature similar market structures. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large-scale vortex patterns in the northern hemisphere's summer. Although Saturn's northern polar vortex is only fully developed during the planet's approximately 29.5-year summer, it has not been observed forming into a ring-like shape feature in previous decades. By analyzing data from the Cassini CMS instrument, we have detected a hexagonal polar vortex forming during Saturn's summer for the first time. The formation of this hexagon within the existing jet stream at a latitude of 17 degrees occurs at a temperature minimum of around 173K in the MSIS model, which is significantly more sensitive to solar energy than previous observations. It has been mathematically proven that this new vortex shape is an exact circle within a hexagon, providing the earliest visual evidence of a Saturnian polar vortex formation. This discovery provides valuable insight for modeling Saturn's polar atmosphere and identifying similar features in other gas giants. It also highlights the importance of observing Saturn's polar atmosphere during its 29.5-year seasonal cycle. The hexagonal polar vortex is an area of further study due to its ring-like shape, which may be a precursor to the formation of an polar stratospheric cloud similar to those found on Neptune and Uranus. This discovery also paves the way for future studies using the extended mission period of the Cassini CMS instrument and upcoming missions such as the JUICE and COMFAR missions. It is predicted that this vortex will continue to develop and eventually form a ring-like shape feature in the northern hemisphere's summer, but further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis. This research is an important contribution to the ongoing study of Saturn's polar atmosphere and its seasonal variations. It is also a significant outcome of the re-analysis of existing data combined with the use of advanced computational modeling. This research provides valuable insights for the broader field of planetary science and the importance of interdisciplinary research. The mechanism driving the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ remains contentious despite its technological implications.  Investigating clean V$_2$O$_3$(0001) surfaces with photoemission and scanning tunneling microscopy, our study reveals that a crystalline surface termination influences the metal-insulator transition temperature (TMI) and microstructure.  Two surface terminations were identified: oxygen-rich surfaces exhibit larger V$_2$O$_3$ domains, higher TMI, and ordered surface dimer structures compared to oxygen-poor surfaces.  Conversely, oxygen-poor surfaces correspond to smaller V$_2$O$_3$ domains, lower TMI, and disordered surface dimer structures.  These findings suggest that both long-range strain and local reordering of surface dimer sites play crucial roles in determining the transition.  A proposed model suggests that clean surfaces undergo a correlated phase transition driven by both surface and bulk dimer ordering, while contamination disrupts this synergy, preventing the metal-insulator transition.  This model is supported by the observation that reordering clean surface dimer structures results in the restoration of the metallic state.  Consequently, surface modification is seen as a key factor in understanding the metal-insulator transitions exhibited by V$_2$O$_3$ and other correlated oxides.  This discovery also highlights the value of surface science in resolving long-standing, fundamental issues in condensed matter physics.  Finally, it is demonstrated that contamination layers in previously studied V$_2$O$_3$ films likely hindered the observation of a correlated bulk and surface dimer-driven transition.  As a result of this research, the term "dead layer" is reevaluated and found to be an inaccurate description, instead reflecting a more complex "surface healing layer".  Furthermore, it is concluded that clean V$_2$O$_3$ interfaces are essential for achieving the metal-insulator transition, implying that interface disorder may also contribute to the transition in other correlated oxides. We employed a hybrid-mixed finite element method to model single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media. Our approach combines the use of continuous and discontinuous pressure variables. A virtual element technique was adapted for the finite element part, allowing for the simulation of fracture networks by mapping them into surfaces within a $H^1$-conforming space. This approach ensures consistent numerical solutions with the given problem's properties. Numerical experiments were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of this method, including simulations of fracture networks with complex geometries and high conductivity. These experiments showed that our hybrid-mixed finite element method can effectively handle a wide range of fracture densities and conductivities. Furthermore, we explored and numerically measured the convergence rates of this method for both continuous and discontinuous pressure variables. These measurements align with the method's predicted convergence rates. Additionally, we investigated the impact of mesh quality on the method's performance, finding that our approach can provide reliable results even with poorly generated meshes. This suggests that our method has a high degree of robustness in terms of mesh tolerance. We also examined the relationship between fracture density and the efficiency of our method, observing that as fractures become more densely packed, more precise mesh generation becomes essential to maintain the method's efficiency. This has significant implications for the field of fractured flow modeling, where flow networks can exhibit a wide range of densities and geometries. This work highlights the method's ability, with appropriate mesh generation, to accurately model even densely packed fractures with complex geometries. This is a significant advancement in the field, as it has become accepted that flow networks can be highly dense and intricately packed, as is the case with fractures within porous media like sandstones. This research provides a critical breakthrough in the development of robust numerical methods for modeling fractured flow in porous media. A graph's edge coloring can be thought of as assigning different colors to edges so that no two adjacent edges share the same color. This concept has been closely linked to other areas of study within graph theory, such as its connections to Ramsey theory and the distribution of chromatic numbers among a particular class of graphs. In previous work, it was hypothesized that a specific subclass of bipartite graphs, those with bipartite degree sequences, would all have edge colorings using a particular number of colors, and this hypothesis was tested on a particular graph within this subclass to find that it does not hold true. The rapid dissemination of computer viruses through the cyber world mirrors the rapid transmission of computer viruses in the aerial environment, prompting us to explore analogous concepts in both domains. By drawing on the principles of anit-virus software, we can develop efficient algorithms to contain the spread of computer viruses. In the aerial domain, we can apply these concepts to minimize the transmission of viruses by regulating the temperature and humidity levels. This can be further optimized by solving an NP-hard problem, and we prove the optimality of a heuristic solution by mapping it to a biologically inspired problem. This research thus bridges the gap between computer science and biology, and we believe it will contribute to both fields. In late October 2019, nationwide protests erupted in Chile, forcing the government to implement strict curfews to maintain order. These enforced isolations resulted in reduced contact rates outside people's homes, leading to increased social interactions within households. We developed an epidemiological model to analyze the spread of the COVID-19 virus during this period, incorporating these non-local reductions in contact rates. Our epidemiological model builds upon existing SIR and SEIR models by accounting for reduced transmission within households, represented by multiple "mini-houses" in a person's social network. We successfully derived a 2D map based on demographic and epidemiological factors from a system of differential equations and confirmed its stability through numerical simulations, mimicking the pre-pandemic equilibrium. Our model also highlights the impact of increased household transmission, suggested by data, as well as the critical threshold for curfew compliance, below which the model enters an unstable equilibrium, resulting in continuous protest-related transmission. Furthermore, we explored how demographic shifts during the protests affected the model's dynamics and identified potential pathways for future outbreaks, even in the absence of explicit population density components. Our study provides a theoretical framework for examining the complex dynamics of social unrest, pandemic spread, and their interconnected phenomena. Finally, we apply our model to analyze the unique factors that contributed to the decline in COVID-19 cases following the initial protests and the distinct curve seen in the later surge during the summer of 2020, with our analysis suggesting that increased temperature-related factors may have accelerated the initial decrease, only to be followed by a more significant increase driven by persistent extrinsic factors. Our work lays the groundwork for extending our model to tackle other social contagion phenomena and highlights the value of epidemiological models in understanding the complex, interconnected nature of modern societal upheavals. We believe that our study offers a unique perspective on the intricate relationship between social unrest, pandemic spread, and curfew policies and underscores the critical role that modeling can play in uncovering the intricate mechanisms governing these interconnected phenomena. We have made the numerical simulations and model solutions available for reproducibility purposes. We utilized observations of the Brackett-$\gamma$ recombination line to assess the accuracy of Star Formation Rates (SFRs) obtained from fitting spectral energy distributions (SEDs). By correlating the observed Brackett-$\gamma$ emission with other tracers of star formation, such as ultraviolet and infrared light, we confirmed that SED-fit SFRs correlate well with the recombination line tracings. However, a potential issue with using recombination lines as a star formation indicator - namely gas excitation variations - was investigated and it was found that while it does impact line brightness, it does not significantly affect SFR determination. Furthermore, by comparing the SFRs derived from different methods, such as UV+IR, we found that the Br$\gamma$-based standard varies with galaxy mass, with the intrinsic scatter decreasing from ~0.6 dex at $10^{9.0}$ $M_{\odot}$ to ~0.2 dex at $10^{10.3}$ $M_{\odot}$. This research provides a framework for evaluating and comparing various SFR estimation methods, including those based on radio recombination lines, and highlights the significance of considering the intrinsic dispersion when comparing SFRs across different galaxy masses. Ultimately, br$\gamma$ is established as a reliable standard for evaluating the performance of SFR fitting methods. Given the complexity involved in fitting spectral energy distributions, such evaluation is a crucial step before applying such methods to the broader astronomical community. The explosive growth of federated learning highlights the significance of collaborative work between distinct organizations for producing robust global models. Nonetheless, numerous companies might hesitate to contribute their data due to privacy concerns, an issue exacerbated when data is sensitive in nature. This problem prompts an inquiry: could it be more efficient to selectively gather data from various firms rather than protecting existing information? This report outlines the Federated Selective Collection Knowledge Amalgamation Approach, a novel methodology that combines data from different sources using a global model. This approach is explained in detail, along with the advantages of FCKA, particularly the reduction of communication costs, decreased label requirements, and enhanced model accuracy. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of FCKA through a comprehensive analysis of theoretical aspects and concrete experiments. The results show that the proposed approach not only protects participant firms' data but also yields significant improvements in global model accuracy. Furthermore, FCKA's efficiency in learning and data efficiency surpass those of conventional federated learning methods. This methodology holds significant practical value and could become a cornerstone for the development of future privacy-enhanced learning frameworks. This research is an initial exploration into the Federated Selective Collection Learning problem, and several open issues are discussed along with potential paths for further exploration. This report concludes by highlighting the potential of FCKA to become an essential tool for data protection companies. This approach could become a fundamental technology for the production of high-quality global models in scenarios where numerous companies are involved. We analyzed possible magnetic cycles in solar-type stars using simulations of rotating convection, as these cycles are likely caused by interactions between rotation and convection. Our simulations covered a range of rotational rates, from normal to reversed rotation patterns, which we refer to as anti-solar rotation. For moderate rotation rates, strong magnetic fields are generated through the $\alpha^2$-dynamos found in slow rotators, and their patterns are stable over time. However, in rapidly rotating stars, these dynamos are overwhelmed by torsional currents, and the stars' magnetic field patterns become unstable. In contrast, anti-solar rotation generally results in weaker magnetic field generation below a certain critical rotation rate. Notably, this decrease is less pronounced in scolloping tacholine regions. The exception is in downflows where anti-solar rotation slightly boosts magnetic field generation, though not enough to form stable magnetic patterns. This increased field generation in downflows may indicate magnetic field enhancement in the interiors of slowly rotating stars. These findings suggest that stars with reversed rotation patterns may exhibit magnetic cycles similar to those of the Sun. Furthermore, this could provide a geometric explanation for the differing magnetic field strengths observed in the northern and southern poles of these stars. Lastly, we propose that stars with reduced rotation rates, but unchanged internal structure, may experience enhanced magnetic field generation in their interiors, potentially leading to magnetic cycles and field patterns visible in their light curves. We analyze the Ankeny-Artin-Murphy conjecture for a specific class of elliptic curves over the rationals, specifically those extending the rationals via a quartic extension through the Galois group $S_4$ or $A_4$, and demonstrate that their rank will rise by at least two in such extensions. This conclusion holds for an infinite subset of such elliptic curves. Furthermore, we investigate the minimal rank behavior within $S_4$ quartic extensions and provide evidence supporting the conjecture that the rank would increase by three in such extensions. Our proof relies on evaluating local contributions at a specific prime, namely 7. This evaluation enables us to determine the behavior within $A_4$ quartic extensions by applying the 2-Selmer switch, thereby establishing a connection between rank changes in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions and their respective quotient groups, $\Delta_2$ and $\Delta_4$. Notably, we find $\Delta_2$ to consist of an infinite number of Passman's quartic fields where the rank exhibits an increase of three. Lastly, I. Chen and Y. Liu have recently become aware of our results and are currently investigating similar problems for larger Galois groups like $S_3$ and $A_3$. Their findings indicate that the Ankeny-Artin-Murphy conjecture would fail for some elliptic curves within these groups, leading to a need to reevaluate the role of 2-Selmer rank growth in such situations and potentially extending the rank increase theorem to a wider context, including the case of cubic extensions. A new class of holographic models has been discovered, featuring sudden, massive wavefronts of entanglement that mark the boundary between two regions of a CFT. These models exhibit two distinct behaviors: in some cases, the wavefronts grow at a constant rate, exceeding the HNS bound, while in others, they conform to the QHEM bound, with entanglement increasing in proportion to the square of time. Both bound-violating and bound-satisfying models demonstrate a surge in both linear growth and quadratic growth of entanglement. We investigate the minimal time required for any initial state on the Bloch ball to become indistinguishable from a target state, obtained through a quantum speed limit (QSL) theorem that utilizes an asymmetry-monotone quantity. Furthermore, we examine how a symmetry-protecting QSL, founded on the variance of the system, relates to its asymmetry-inducing counterpart, both theoretically and through associated examples. Moreover, we determine the specific conditions under which both types of QSL bounds converge to the well-known Helstrom limit for distinguishability of pure states. Additionally, we establish that in scenarios where the variance-based QSL performs better than the Helstrom limit, the asymmetry-based QSL outperforms it over states with sufficient rotational symmetry around a specific axis. Building on these findings, we derive a general formula for calculating the optimal rotation angles that minimize indistinguishability time for any pure or mixed state on the Bloch ball. These results provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing the complex trade-off between quantum state discrimination delay and accuracy within the confines of the Bloch ball. Consequently, this study extends the current understanding of quantum state discrimination in the Bloch ball to its most general form, encompassing not only pure states but also squeezed states and any initial state on the Bloch ball. Although deep learning-based medical image segmentation has made significant progress in recent years, its effectiveness is greatly limited by the requirement for extensive labeling of training images. Semi-supervised learning has the potential to utilize a small labeled dataset in combination with a large, unlabeled image database to reduce this burden. Domain adaptation plays a crucial role in semi-supervised learning when annotating images in the training and testing domains is impractical. This study assumes that two testing domains, T1 and T2, represent analogous anatomical structures and, as such, domain adaptation is feasible between them with minimal additional annotation. To leverage a large, unlabeled dataset from domain T1, this study employs Contrastive Semi-supervised learning to expand the labeled dataset with similar transformations from the same domain. It utilizes a domain-specific latent space to achieve this, with a view to conducting a similar segmentation task. The model is then employed to generate a labeled dataset for domain T2, based on the learned features, with reduced annotation required. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms alternative semi-supervised learning approaches while delivering comparable performance to fully supervised domain-specific segmentation. Rank metric and Gabriel metric have gained significance in the development of reliable digital data storage and communication systems, particularly those employing nested or side-facing structuring, to counteract malicious attacks from an adversary. A crucial component in such systems is the decoding algorithm, responsible for converting rank or Gabriel metric errors into correctable binary errors. This paper focuses on optimizing the decoding of rank or Gabriel metric errors in systems with a symmetric structure, a feature that was previously unexplored. By establishing an equivalence with the Gabriel metric decoding problem, this paper develops efficient and optimized decoding methods that take into account the system's symmetric properties, leading to a reduction in the number of necessary computations by a factor of at least $\sqrt{2^k}$ compared to previous methods, where $k$ represents the rank or Gabriel metric dimension. Specifically, for $k=3$, a further optimized method yields a computation reduction by a factor of at least $8$, demonstrating the potential for significant performance gains. This research provides a framework for enhancing the efficient decoding of errors in rank metric and Gabriel metric systems. Using a combination of computational models for the early stages of high-mass star formation and radiative transfer simulations of outgoing radiation and dust, we shed light on the physical development of massive protostars. Our analysis reveals that massive protostars likely emerge from a stage in which multiple small-scale collapse regions, or "cores," are independently forming stars. As these cores combine due to the gravitational pull of the growing protostar at their center, they take on the shape of a highly irregular "halo." Cores then accumulate at the edge of this halo, eventually coalescing into even more substantial "bowls" or "depressions." This process of accrual is thought to set the stage for mergers between nearby protostellar objects, which can lead to the formation of dense "collar-like" features. These features can, in turn, give rise to distinctive hourglass-shaped structures. Our research also shows that the accretion rates in these systems are often quite high, resulting in the formation of a substantial amount of angular momentum. This excess angular momentum then needs to be relieved, which can lead to the ejection of massive protostellar jets. The automatic processing of emotion-related texts depends heavily on the quality of their annotations.  Despite significant investment in developing annotation tools and guides, published datasets still contain numerous errors.  One reason for this is that annotators struggle to consider the context when determining the underlying emotion associated with a given text.  Our proposed solution to this issue involves leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT to guide the annotation process.  We tested this approach by re-annotating a subset of emotionally charged sentences from the EMO14K dataset, using BERT to inform our results.  Our findings indicate that our method yields annotations at least 20% more accurate than existing BERT-free approaches.  We also observed that context plays a crucial role in predicting the underlying emotion, accounting for up to 18% of all corrections made.  Our code and data are openly available for reproducibility purposes.  Our proposed method can be applied across other text classification tasks that rely on semantic annotations, such as sentiment analysis and topic modeling.  We make available open-source versions of our pre-trained models and annotation tools for these tasks.  Our research also highlights the importance of conducting thorough evaluations when assessing the performance of pre-trained language models on emotion-related tasks.  We explored alternative approaches to our proposed BERT-supported annotation process, including using BERT to re-rank existing annotations and combining it with active learning techniques.  Our results suggest that these approaches, although intuitive, either underperformed or failed to improve upon our method.  We discuss potential avenues for further research to address the challenges associated with annotating emotion-related texts.  Our work underscores the value of collaborations between natural language processing experts and mathematicians in evaluating and refining annotation processes.  We outline open issues and potential research directions for the NLP community, including developing more effective methods for leveraging contextual information and alternative models like transformer-XL and XLNet.  We highlight the importance of balancing the quality of annotations with the efficiency of the annotation process, particularly in large-scale annotation settings.  We discuss the applicability of our proposed approach to emotion-related taxonomies and the importance of considering valence in annotation processes.  Our work sets the stage for exploring the interplay between context and emotion in NLP tasks, the design of more effective annotation tools, and the development of models capable of capturing this interplay.  We anticipate that our research will prompt the creation of higher-quality emotion-related datasets, leading to advancements in emotion-aware applications that rely on semantic annotations, such as hate speech detection and microexpression analysis

Our theoretical analysis of the TMDCs' response to temperature changes is detailed, revealing that the magnetic ordering induces opposing spin-polarized thermal conductivity components that vary with temperature. Moreover, we identify that the p-type thermal conductivity component undergoes a significant transformation from a negative to a positive value when temperature increases, an effect that is heavily dependent on the spin polarization and alignment. Notably, the odd parity of the spin-polarized thermal conductivity tensor ensures that the p-type component remains symmetrical across crystal axes, and we demonstrate that TMDCs with varying thicknesses exhibit consistent magnetothermal properties. Additionally, we propose feasible experimental protocols to measure the spin-polarized thermal conductivity components in TMDCs. Our findings provide a fundamental understanding of the spin-polarized magnetothermal effect in TMDCs and suggest their potential for applications in spin-polarized thermal transport and magnetic field-free magnetic data storage. Furthermore, we observe that MoSe2 covered by WSe2 exhibits a significant thermal spin-polarized output ratio, a valuable property that could be harnessed to develop efficient spin-polarized devices. Additionally, we examine the effects of lattice vibrations and electron-electron interactions on the magnetothermal properties of TMDCs. Our research contributes to the exploration of spin-polarized thermal conductivity in TMDCs and highlights the influence of proximity effects on their magnetic and thermal conductivity behavior. Investigating these effects will be crucial for uncovering the broader implications for spin-polarized conductivity in these materials. Furthermore, we suggest that TMDCs could be used as magnetic field-free magnetic data storage materials, with the potential for implementation in spin-polarized electronics. Our analysis also reveals that the magnetothermal effect in TMDCs can be controlled through temperature changes, exhibiting positive output ratios that could be useful for thermal spin-polarization. We investigate how the electron spill-out and nonlocal response of electrons within a metal impact the behavior of gap-plasmons. Our study utilizes a semi-analytical approach and takes into consideration the effects of both the electron spill-out and nonlocality, examining their influence on gap-plasmons in the limit where the gap becomes extremely narrow. A relativistically small gap can lead to a divergent plasmon frequency when nonlocal effects are considered, and we find that this divergence is mitigated by the electron spill-out's influence when a certain parameter is taken into account. This parameter, which measures the distance between electrons within the metal relative to the gap's width, helps to mitigate the nonlocal effect's impact on plasmons and indicates that the electron spill-out's influence on gap-plasmons can dominate that of nonlocality. A theoretical model is developed to understand the behavior of gap-plasmons in relation to their spatial extension and the method of excitation used, and we find that our results are consistent with prior studies on surface-plasmons. A simple model is also proposed to incorporate the effects of both electron spill-out and nonlocality into a quasi-static approach, and this model demonstrates that both effects must be considered in the study of gap-plasmons due to their significant impact on the plasmon's behavior. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response of electrons must be considered in the study of gap-plasmons, and that their combined influence results in a more accurate understanding of the behavior of these phenomena than can be gained through the study of surface-plasmons. As a result, a more comprehensive theoretical model is necessary to accurately describe the behavior of gap-plasmons. Due to the widespread use of metal nanostructures in applications involving gap-plasmons, such as quantum dot fluorescence and SERS, it is essential from a practical standpoint to thoroughly understand the behavior of these phenomena. Finally, our research suggests that a greater consideration must be given to both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response of electrons within a metal in the study of plasmon-mediated interactions, as these effects can result in a significant enhancement or reduction of the plasmon's energy transfer to another system. However, the reliability of normalization can be compromised when the lambda calculus is subjected to diversions, ambiguities, or barbers paradoxes in termination proofs. To address this vulnerability, this work introduces three robust normalization techniques for the Calculus of Constructions, ensuring that types that can be proved are always valid. Furthermore, these techniques prevent the derivation of contradictory types from assumption lists with no inherent paradoxes. We explore and compare the properties of these techniques, including their impact on module composition and type abstraction. One of these techniques demonstrates particular efficiency in terms of step count. An implementation in the CoC Coq proof assistant is also discussed, along with the performance gains it exhibits. Ultimately, this research confirms that robust normalization is essential in type theories with inhabitation and module composition and identifies areas for further optimization in its implementation. In addition, this work is relevant to other research involving termination proofs in type theories. In a companion paper, we explore connections between type abstractions and normalization. One notable contribution involves demonstrating that the applicability of a type abstraction operator can be determined by a variant of robust normalization. This connection between type abstraction and normalization paves the way for the development of more complex type operators that can be securely applied only to types that can be proved. As GPU computing advances, so does its potential to tackle complex, memory-intensive tasks efficiently. However, achieving high performance on GPUs is hindered by limited memory accessibility, primarily resulting from inadequate memory allocation strategies. Current memory allocators for GPUs are often slow due to their sequential nature or lack of parallel support, resulting in suboptimal code fragmentation and wasted memory space. To overcome these challenges, we present DynaSOAr, a novel memory allocator specifically designed for object-based programming on GPUs, utilizing inter-object space to minimize memory usage and promote coalesced memory access. By leveraging multiple threads and a dynamic free list, DynaSOAr achieves efficient memory allocation and reduction of fragmentation, outperforming existing memory allocators by up to 5.5 times for sequential applications and 3.5 times for parallel ones. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's memory usage is consistently lower than existing methods, often by as much as 12 times for parallel applications. The allocator's performance and memory efficiency improvements are attributed to its effective suppression of memory contention, resulting in significant boosts to application performance. The average performance gain for tested applications ranges from 1.2 to 14.4 times, with some parallel applications experiencing a gain as high as 20 times. DynaSOAr's efficient memory allocation and reduced fragmentation enable better exploitation of available memory, resulting in outstanding performance on GPU systems. The proposed allocator serves as a suitable companion to object-based programming on GPUs and is an important development, given the growing prevalence of such programming models. The DynaSOAr allocator is an innovative solution that is suitable for a wide range of applications and has been successfully integrated into various object-based GPU programs. The challenges and proposed solutions presented in this research are equally relevant to other parallel computing platforms, such as distributed systems, and the DynaSOAr allocator's performance and memory usage could serve as a baseline for similar memory allocators for these platforms. A comprehensive theoretical framework for describing Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in complex superconducting systems has been developed using a 2$H$-matrix approach. This method leverages a robust and efficient quasi-particle Green's function technique to examine the interaction between localized magnetic impurities and superconducting hosts. Specifically, a detailed study was conducted on Mn adatoms and Mn clusters situated on the Nb(110) surface to better understand their influence on superconducting proximity effects. For a single adatom positioned at a high-symmetry site, a hinge site showed significantly reduced YSR state splitting due to spin-orientation-dependent effects. Conversely, when the adatom was placed at a bridge site, YSR state splitting was significantly increased, presenting a potential for spin-orientation-dependent phenomena. Additionally, simulations of Mn dimer and trimer structures revealed distinct YSR state splitting patterns, serving as evidence for long-range superconducting proximity effects. These findings are corroborated by experimental data from tunnel spectroscopy, offering valuable insights for the design of complex magnetic systems within superconducting hosts. Ultimately, this research paves the way for exploring other systems involving magnetic ions on the surface of superconducting materials. A notable mention is the recent work by the same authors and their colleagues featured in a preceding publication, where the influence of localized magnetic moments on superconducting proximity effects was investigated through tunnel spectroscopy of Mn adatoms and clusters on the Nb(110) surface. The current study delves deeper into the underlying physics by applying a first-principles approach to analyze the quasi-particle states of Mn adatoms and clusters within the superconducting Nb matrix. A significant disparity was observed in the splitting patterns of YSR states when comparing experimental data and simulations based on a general quasi-particle Green's function technique. To resolve this discrepancy, a 2$H$-matrix approach was employed to examine the individual contributions of Nb $s$- and $d$-bands to the superconducting properties. By using this approach, the influence of Mn magnetization on the splitting of YSR states was accurately reproduced through simulations, thus demonstrating the intricacies involved in designing magnetic systems within superconducting hosts. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from 48 to 80 days, with a likely age of 65 days. The main achievement of this research is the identification of a particular infinite graph whose ramsey property relates to upper richness in an unexpected manner. To study Quantum Electrodynamics in strong-field environments, researchers have been searching for a suitable positron source. We posit that a highly polarized positron beam could be achieved by focusing laser light on polarized film targets in a state of relativistic transparency. Numerical modeling indicates that a positron density of approximately 10^17 cm^-3 with over 99% polarization could be attained when the target is irradiated with an intense laser field in the Quantum Electrodynamics regime. Furthermore, we demonstrate through analytical scaling that increasing the target thickness or the number of femtosecond pulses does not significantly impact positron polarization. However, both factors do influence the total positron count, which could reach the desired level of 10^9 positrons with appropriate conditions. We propose using a positron source with high polarization to investigate matter-electron interaction in a state of high transparency. Specifically, we predict that the transmission coefficient of a highly transparent state can exceed unity by a factor of about 10 when polarized positrons are involved. Consequently, the expected burst of dense polarized positrons may have far-reaching implications for both high-energy physics and quantum optics. Furthermore, we suggest that the proposed source could be relevant for examining quantum flux tubes and the proposed production of electron-positron pairs through strong x-ray focusing. Ultimately, this concept may also pave the way for investigating nonperturbative QED effects in a new context. We also discuss potential experimental verification of our theoretical predictions at the HiLASE and NELI2 centers with a proposed positron characterization facility. The proposed model can be validated through the observation of quasiresonant radiation at the 511 keV energy level as well as through the collection and analysis of dense polarized positrons. The feasibility of the experiment is supported by existing evidence from the two-film-target experiment and modeling of the multi-film-target setup. We outline the necessary parameters for the experiment, which can be carried out using existing laser technology and without the need for the development of new technology. The proposed experiment offers a unique opportunity to explore the properties of strong-field Quantum Electrodynamics in a new paradigm. The expected results of the experiment will also contribute significantly to the development of experimental models for research on strong-field Quantum Electrodynamics in strong x-ray fields. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Music has long been a primary means of self-expression through various forms, including vocal performances that utilize melody, rhythm, and harmony. Although technology offers numerous ways to create music, few systems effectively incorporate natural language inputs to facilitate music generation. This disparity exists because natural language processing techniques struggle to capture the intricate elements of music notation, composition, and performance, which are inherently different from natural language in their structure and function. In an effort to bridge this gap, a new dataset called the Pied Piper Dataset is introduced, which utilizes data from search engines to link natural language queries to musical compositions and their underlying structures. This dataset serves as the foundation for a music generation model that can be experienced through a VR interface, allowing users to input natural language instructions to a virtual guide who then interprets these instructions and performs the resulting musical composition on a virtual instrument. This model, which incorporates a range of advanced technologies like neural networks, virtual reality, and machine learning, represents a significant step towards creating a more accessible and user-friendly music composition tool. This paper provides a detailed exploration of the Pied Piper Dataset, the music generation model, and our VR prototyping approach, highlighting both the innovative aspects and the challenging issues that arise when integrating natural language understanding with music performance. This is further illustrated by our experience building a Pied Piper Music Generator, which is now available for public exploration on the Unity Store and the GitHub repository. This music generation model is unique in its use of natural language inputs to create complex musical compositions, and as such, it has the potential to inspire a wider audience to explore music composition, while also offering a engaging musical experience for anyone to enjoy. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity in core sizes among starless and protostellar cores within this region.  Using core size and mass as key indicators, our analysis shows a significant correlation between the two, with a slope of 0.55$\pm$0.20, indicating that larger cores in the Dragon have higher mass counterparts.  Our findings also indicate a notable difference in core mass-to-size ratios between starless and protostellar cores, with protostellar cores exhibiting a greater ratio by a factor of two to three.  This distinction supports previous research indicating that massive star formation is more likely to originate from more expansive cores.  With an eye on the Dragon, research suggests that further investigation into this particular infrared dark cloud is warranted, as it may provide a unique glimpse into the early stages of high-mass star formation. This paper reports on an in-depth analysis of 80 UHE neutrinos detected by the IceCube detector and their connection to UHECR arrival directions as recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory. Specifically, it examines if there are UHECR sources or neutrino sources associated with UHECR spatial patterns, such as clusters and hotspots. The statistical significance of these associations is calculated under various hypotheses, including those of spatial correlations with sources like Active Galactic Nuclei, as well as with neutrino sources, which could be supernovae or other objects. The findings support the existence of associations with UHECR sources and neutrino sources at a 2.9σ level, and specifically with neutrino sources at 4.0σ, and slightly reduce the density of UHECR sources by a factor of about two-and-a-half. The paper also presents a novel approach to investigate neutrino-UHECR spatial cross-correlations. If such correlations are real, various right ascension and declination-based splits show significant deviations at a 3σ level. The discovered spatial concentrations of UHECRs are primarily aimed at the Centaurus A galaxy, which is about 25 million light-years from Earth, and at two other AGN located at much greater distances. The probability of randomly selecting such concentrated directions by chance is extremely low, at less than 0.004. The findings of this study provide valuable insights that can be used by future, multi-component cosmic-ray experiments like the AugerPlus and the Askaryan Radio Array, as well as by next-generation neutrino detectors like the IceCube Gen2 and the PUEO, to identify the sources of UHECRs and neutrinos. By employing radiolength interferometry and global voltage measurements at millimeter wavelengths, the molecular structure of ethynyl cyclopentadiene has been determined, revealing two rotational isomers instead of the initially predicted three-dimensional structure. This finding is further supported by an analysis of ethynyl benzene data, with the result that two of its rotamers have frequencies very close to those of CHCCH. The detection of cyclopentadiene's isomers, along with its parent molecule, provides insight into the molecular synthesis process and suggests that cyclopentadiene undergoes dimerization to form CHCCH in the TMC-1 cloud. Abundances for these molecules are found to be in the order of 10 to the power of minus 9 in units of density. This abundance ratio of ethynyl benzene to cyclopentadiene is consistent with the dimerization hypothesis. This discovery of isomers in the TMC-1 cloud offers a unique glimpse into the molecular synthesis processes occurring within this specific molecular environment. This environment is characterized by low temperatures and the presence of unusual N2-CO and CCH-CN cycle abundance patterns. This abundance pattern of CCH over CN, which is observed in cyclic molecules, is thought to be influenced by the strength of intermolecular interactions between N2 and CO. This hypothesis is to be tested by observing these molecules in NGC 1333, a more evolved star-forming region. This evaluation will also consider any potential biases introduced by the detection of a molecule's parent and dimer forms through the analysis of CHCCH and CN/CCH lines in these regions. This analysis will provide a more comprehensive understanding of how molecular structures are formed in different environments. This knowledge can be applied to the study of other molecules in TMC-1, such as those containing a cyclopentadiene ring, with a possible dimerization origin. In neural machine translation, the majority of systems employ a sequence-to-sequence framework with attention to generate target texts. However, existing methods typically only consider previously produced source sentences and a limited history of target sentences. This research introduces a novel focus mechanism to the target sentence generation model, allowing it to effectively utilize the entire target context, including future segments. Experiments using a large parallel corpus showed that our proposed method significantly outperforms the baseline model, resulting in improvements of 0.17 ($p<0.01$) and 0.10 ($p<0.05$) in BLEU scores on average for source sentences of lengths 10 and 20, respectively. Moreover, our method proves particularly beneficial for longer source sentences, yielding a 0.54 ($p<0.01$) BLEU score increase for those with lengths greater than 20. This approach also exhibits comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on smaller parallel corpora, indicating that our proposed method effectively balances data efficiency and linguistic plausibility. Our implementation showcases the greatest effectiveness among compared methods when look-ahead focus is integrated with a source-guided generation strategy, achieving a 0.45 ($p<0.01$) BLEU score improvement over the baseline on standard test sets. This method's efficacy is further validated through unsampled translation experiments, revealing that our proposed approach produces target sentences with higher BLEU scores when evaluated against a larger set of ground truth target sentences. This supports the hypothesis that look-ahead focus helps generate more precise target sentences. This research introduces novel focus mechanisms and integrates them into a sequence-to-sequence framework with attention, along with a data-driven method to evaluate the proposed methods' ability to generate accurate target sentences from any given source sentence. This evaluation framework's utility is demonstrated by identifying the optimal method for a large parallel corpus without the need for additional training. This evaluation framework's utility extends to unsupervised translation scenarios, enabling the evaluation of generated target sentences with real-valued labels. This research introduces three focus mechanism variants, including look-ahead focus, look-behind focus, and uniform focus. Uniform focus combines the strengths of look-ahead and look-behind focus, leveraging target sentence segments on both sides. This variant outperforms the baseline model by 0.08 ($p<0.05$) in terms of BLEU scores on average for source sentences of lengths up to 20. Look-behind focus proves less effective than look-ahead focus but still outperforms the baseline model by 0.04

The rapid growth of ridesharing services has generated substantial amounts of location data, enabling the creation of detailed urban road maps through detection methods. Researchers have proposed several algorithms in the past to tackle this problem, but most are primarily optimal for the specific datasets used in their development. A more universally effective approach would provide guaranteed performance regardless of data size. This study introduces two novel detection methods for urban road networks based on ridesharing routes and location data, leveraging the theory of semi-supervised learning to derive implicit information from urban navigation patterns. The first approach, called optimal semi-supervised detection, maximizes the number of correctly identified roads by combining ridesharing data, location patterns, and existing map information. The second method, called multi-round semi-supervised detection, iteratively refines its predictions by integrating new information at each stage.
